title: Out-of-the-box ideas for school lunches
text:
Are you looking for some fresh ideas for what to include in your children's school lunch?

Dietician and nutritionist Heidi Sze has you covered with these nutritious and delicious recipes that will liven up their lunch boxes.

This pasta salad is great alternative to sandwiches for school lunches, but keep it chilled with a frozen drink or pop the container in a cooler bag. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

This pasta salad, with slow-roasted tomatoes, fresh corn and basil, is a salute to the warmer seasons.

It's packed with cannellini beans for extra fibre and protein and is an easily adaptable recipe, too, so if you want to sneak some extra greens into your kids' lunches, add a big handful of rocket.

Using leftover roasted pumpkin adds the perfect flavour and texture to the smash. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

This recipe quickly smashes chickpeas together with a bunch of ingredients to make a filling for sandwiches or wraps. It's nourishing and satisfying and will last for several days in the fridge.

Leftover roasted pumpkin brings sweetness and softness to the smash, while the gherkins add a vibrant crunch.

You can also experiment with different flavour combinations based on your preferences and what you have on hand.

Heidi's wholemeal pikelets provide a lovely base for sweet toppings, such as butter and jam, or maple syrup. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Heidi fondly recalls her mum making her pikelets as an after-school treat, and it's a tradition she has kept going with her own children.

This recipe uses spelt wholemeal flour, which provides a heartier and healthier base, but you can regular wholemeal flour if you prefer.

You can also make the pikelets dairy-free by replacing the cow's milk with dairy-free milk, and the butter with coconut oil.

title: Curtin University warns proposed merger 'solves problems we don't have'
text:
Curtin University's vice-chancellor says a planned merger of three Western Australian universities "solves problems that we don't have and creates problems that we don't need".

The WA government's decision to push ahead with a business case to merge Curtin University, Murdoch University and the University of Western Australia (UWA) has sparked fierce debate, with all three universities and many of their staff raising concerns.

But WA's Tertiary Education Minister Tony Buti said the state's universities were in a "race to the bottom" and that many students had told him they were receiving a "substandard education".

The WA government will undertake a business case into the potential amalgamation of three of the state's public universities. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

The government argues a mega university catering to around 120,000 students would keep the sector competitive while helping them attract more students and investment.

"There's a hyper-competition between our universities. We want to ensure that our universities are world-class, that is what this is all about," Mr Buti said.

'Solution looking for a problem'

But Curtin University's vice-chancellor Harlene Hayne said the proposal amounted to a "solution looking for a problem", slamming it as a costly process that aimed to "fix something that is not broken".

Graduates' satisfaction with degrees at record lows Australian students are less satisfied with their university degrees than ever before, according to a long-running survey.

Professor Hayne hit back at Mr Buti's claims WA's universities were in a race to the bottom.

"If you actually look at the data, 90 per cent of the students who graduate from a Western Australian university get a job within six months and the employers rate them amongst the best in Australia. I don't think that's the definition of a sub-par degree," she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Professor Hayne also responded to figures that revealed five individual eastern state universities each received more of Australia’s research funding than all four WA public universities combined.

She laid the blame for that partly at the WA government's feet, saying many of those universities received seed funding from their state governments, allowing them to generate more research funding as part of a "virtuous cycle".

She also disputed figures provided by the government that showed the number of students completing undergraduate degrees ranged from 49 per cent at Murdoch to 75 per cent at UWA, saying that was based on "an old-fashioned" benchmark that required students to finish a degree within six years.

Professor Hayne rejected the idea that four public universities was too many for WA's growing population, saying it had fewer than other states and many other countries on a per capita basis.

UWA, pictured, would be merged with Curtin and Murdoch universities under the proposal. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Sector 'punching well below its weight'

Among those arguing in favour of the merger is Mark Barnaba, who will chair a steering committee that will provide expert advice throughout the business case process to the government.

Mark Barnaba says the business case will be respect the customs and histories of the universities. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

He said the state's university sector was "punching well below its weight" and the merger was about what was best for all WA taxpayers.

The government's big changes to universities, explained The government will spend an extra $3.6 billion over a decade on new university places, but some are warning the money could be wasted.

Mr Barnaba told 102.5 ABC Perth the most optimistic cost-benefit estimate put the benefit of the amalgamation at 15 times the transition cost, but that the final price tag would be determined by the business case.

He disputed Professor Hayne's claims the merger would result in job losses, saying it was about creating stronger universities.

"I just don't understand, when the basis for this is a stronger university sector and fundamental tertiary and economic reform, why there wouldn't be growth and further opportunity," he said.

Mr Barnaba said the committee, which was expected to present its findings to the government by mid-2027, would respect the history and customs of the universities throughout the process.

Backlash from staff

More than two-thirds of WA public university staff oppose mergers, according to a recent survey by the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU).

More than three-quarters of Curtin University staff were against a three-way merger, with 66 and 68 per cent of UWA and Murdoch staff in opposition, respectively.

More than three-quarters of Curtin University staff are against a three-way merger, according to a survey. (ABC News: Hugh Sando.)

NTEU WA division secretary Scott Fitzgerald, a professor at Curtin, said public universities existed to serve students, staff and the wider community.

"Any decision about their future should be through that focus, not a simplistic approach that puts profits over people," he said.

"Staff want real governance reform and an end to the corporatisation of their universities. A merger would double down on an approach that has already failed them."

title: Butters suggests changes to AFL player movement 'wouldn't be a bad thing'
text:
Zak Butters says he contemplated going public with his planned move home to Victoria while playing out his final season at Port Adelaide.

The Western Bulldogs unveiled their star recruit at Whitten Oval today following his blockbuster move as a free agent on a nine-year deal worth $2 million a season.

With a year left on his contract at the Power, Butters knew he was leaving Alberton following open conversations with the club at the end of last season.

He discussed going public with his plans with manager Peter Lenton.

"I definitely contemplated and thought about that," the midfielder said.

"But I think the AFL landscape isn't probably quite ready for it."

NRL players can sign deals with rival clubs once they enter the final year of their contract or earlier if given permission.

Butters unveiled by Bulldogs after 'megadeal' Zak Butters is finally unveiled as a Western Bulldogs player as Port Adelaide receives four first-round picks in a five-team mega trade ticked off by the league.

Deals are often announced during the season.

The AFL system is more restrictive, with listed players coming off contract only able to officially move in the off-season through trade, free agency, drafts and the supplemental selection period.

"The way I play football and the way I train, I feel like I'd be able to show up and front up and do it," Butters said.

"But definitely, I feel like in the future, I couldn't see why it wouldn't be a bad thing."

Butters, a three-time All Australian, was strongly courted by the Bulldogs, Geelong, Collingwood and Richmond throughout the year.

Geelong was viewed as the frontrunner for his signature, but Butters denied he or his management ever indicated to the Cats they were his first preference.

The ball magnet insisted he never completely made up his mind until returning home to his family property at Darley, west of Melbourne, after the Power's season had ended.

"I guess I probably took my time to do that," Butters said.

"It's a pretty long contract and it's probably the rest of my career so I wanted to make sure I get it right.

"I probably leaned towards different clubs at different stages but, ultimately, I got to where I wanted to get to."

Zak Butters (right) pictured with Bulldogs supporter Hunter Zerafa. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

The Bulldogs pulled heavily on Butters's heartstrings in their pitch, drawing on his boyhood fandom for the club.

A handwritten letter from 11-year-old Hunter Zerafa, accompanied by a 20-cent coin taped inside, begging Butters to pick the Bulldogs revived childhood memories.

"I thought back to when I was younger and loving Bulldogs players and looking up to them and coming down to open trainings," Butters said.

"I used to have birthday parties at Whitten Oval when I was a kid.

"I've still got the letter at home, and the 20 cents is still in there. I might have to invest it."

AAP

title: Job losses likely at remote island mine as costs nearly double due to flooding
text:
Job losses are likely at South 32's manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory as the operation battles years of flooding impacts and skyrocketing production costs.

The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) mine has begun consultations with staff.

The ABC understands it needs to cut $129 million from the business in response to costs increasing by more than 80 per cent in recent years.

The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in March 2024, but it is understood multiple wet seasons and persistent seepage of groundwater into the pits are also responsible.





Mining pits on Groote Eylandt filled with water after Cyclone Megan in 2024. (Supplied) GEMCO is planning to spend about $100 million on new water infrastructure in the next two years if it receives regulatory approvals.

A South32 spokesperson said in a statement the company would make changes to strengthen its long-term viability and was speaking to workers.

"GEMCO has completed an internal review in response to a more challenging operating environment and increased cost pressures, and has begun implementing changes designed to strengthen the long-term sustainability of the business," the spokesperson said.

"The review forms part of a program focused on improving structures, systems and processes and ensuring GEMCO is well positioned to operate successfully into the future. As part of this work, GEMCO has reviewed its workforce requirements and commenced consultation with employees and contractors who will potentially be impacted.

" This is not something we take lightly and our priority is to support affected employees through the process, including exploring redeployment opportunities where possible. "

Unions watching closely

Officials from two separate unions representing workers at GEMCO told the ABC they believed office staff would likely be the target of redundancies.

A spokesperson for the NT branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union said it was closely monitoring the situation to see if blue-collar workers were affected.

Union officials were told South 32 management would provide staff with more information about the redundancies by the end of the week.

According to GEMCO's enterprise bargaining agreement, the company must consult with workers before making any significant organisational changes.

The bargaining agreement is due to expire at the end of 2027.

The MV Anikitos was loaded with 41,000 tonnes of manganese ore when it crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt. (Supplied)

The island's wharf was destroyed in 2024 when Tropical Cyclone Megan pushed a loaded bulk carrier into the structure during high tides.

Heavy rainfall damaged the mine's pits, a critical bridge and several roads.

Exports from the island did not restart until 2025.

Mining is expected to conclude on the island within the next 10 years, according to the local Aboriginal land council.

title: Kaniva wants to be known as an EV charging hub
text:
On a long stretch of highway roughly halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide is a farming town hoping to cement its reputation as an electric vehicle (EV) charging must-see.

The western Victorian farming town of Kaniva, with a population of roughly 800 people, already has 10 Tesla Superchargers behind its quaint country pub.

The global tech giant has submitted plans to the local council to install another eight, and publican Bob Cane couldn't be happier.

Kaniva is home to 10 EV charging sites, with plans to install another eight. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"It's about bringing people to Kaniva, connecting them with a classic, quintessential Australian classic town," Mr Cane said.

Painted sheep have adorned the streets of Kaniva since 2012. (ABC News: Martin Boulton)

Kaniva currently markets itself as the first and last highway town in Victoria, the gateway to the Wimmera Mallee Silo Art Trail and the "home of Sheep Art".

Mr Cane said the chargers were invigorating the town and adding another string to its economy.

"When they plug in their car, what are they going to do? [They will] go for a walk into town, get a coffee, grab a hamburger," he said.

Bob Cane is hoping the new Supercharger stations will be up and running before Christmas. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

" The town benefits … that's a big plus for tourism because it puts Kaniva on the map. "

The Windmill Cafe owner Jemma Hill said the chargers had been a boon for the town.

"They [travellers] stop, they come over, they grab their lunch and their coffee, they come into town," she said.

"It's creating extra foot traffic within the town, which is fantastic, makes it feel very alive."

Jemma Hill says the current EV chargers have helped her business. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

A hub for travellers

The existing chargers are a lifesaver for some travellers already tackling the trek between Melbourne and Adelaide.

"We do this trip a few times a year … If we didn't have this, we couldn't get [to Melbourne]," Tom Beresford said.

Kaniva is home to about 800 people. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

West Wimmera Shire Council deputy mayor Helen Hobbs said the site, which has been open for about nine months, had already made a difference in the town.

"That has actually given people like the bakery confidence to invest," Cr Hobbs said.

"To have a brand new bakery with seating for 100 people, it's beyond anything I could have imagined."

Helen Hobbs says the EV chargers have brought outside investment into the town. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Need for more infrastructure

EV sales doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council of Australia.

The council's Aman Gaur attributed the jump to cheaper EVs, rising fuel costs and improved charging networks.

"We're now up to 4,200 charging locations across Australia and over 11,000 connectors," Mr Gaur said.

"Charging stations have definitely been increasing in Victoria and the number of connectors has also been following suit."

Ampol this month paid $225 million to buy Evie, one of the country's largest charging networks.

Milad Haghani says if EV demand continues to grow at the same pace, charging infrastructure will have to catch up. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

University of Melbourne associate professor of urban resilience and mobility Milad Haghani said charging infrastructure would have a serious job keeping up if the EV sales boom continued.

"It's hard to predict whether or not the spike in demand that we have observed this year is going to be sustainable," he said.

"But if even a fraction of this demand continues into the future, that means that the infrastructure has some catching up to do."

Public chargers have rarely had queues, he said, but that could change as more people buy EVs.

"If we wait for the demand … [to grow more] before we invest in the infrastructure, we may lag far behind," he said.

The waiting game

The West Wimmera Shire Council has published Tesla's planning application online while it assesses the proposal.

The application says the upgrade would cost $250,000 and that the existing 10-stall site, open for about nine months, has exceeded the company's expectations.

A traffic report filed with the application says 10 to 20 EVs charge at the site each day, with holidays a natural peak period.

Residents have until next Monday to lodge an objection to Tesla's plans.

Mr Cane said it's about making the town ready for whatever happens next.

"While they're here, they've got the availability of these Superchargers and we're ready for the future," he said.

title: The extra stripe that's landed Australian retailer White Fox in court
text:
When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it is part of its trademark.

The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration.

The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia.

According to court documents, Adidas accuses White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple clothing items and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing.

Adidas claims this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark, which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years.

White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year.

A White Fox Boutique advertisement seen on the back of a bus. (Supplied)

According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied clothing with four parallel stripes on it since March this year, including advertisements on buses, bus stops and on social media.

Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do.

Adidas further claimed White Fox used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies.

An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. (Supplied)

It alleges White Fox's actions are likely to cause damage to its reputation.

In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.

He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands, including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein.

Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe.

"Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a Queensland University of Technology lecturer, said.

He explained a 2023 High Court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trademark, compared to the impression created by the sign used.

"Counting stripes is only the start," he said.

Adidas trademark at risk

The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949, but was not trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had trademarked the same logo.

Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1,600 euros ($AUD2,500) for the logo, which it has extensively protected ever since.

In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar".

However, University of Technology Sydney School of Law senior lecturer Sarah Hook said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions.

In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design.

Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK, and the High Court ultimately ruled the trademark was invalid.

"That's because the court said that the trademark itself wasn't very clear and distinct about what it would cover and which variations it would cover," Dr Hook said.

Adidas loses court battle Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas.

University of Melbourne intellectual property law studies director Benjamin Hopper said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it had to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

"For example, if I owned a company that sold chairs, armchairs, lounge chairs, dining room chairs, office chairs, theatre chairs, it was just chairs and I called it The Chair Company or I called it Chairs and I said, 'I want to get a trademark for chairs,' it would just completely not be distinctive because the word chair has zero capacity to distinguish my chair in the marketplace from the chairs of other traders," he said.

"The argument here is that, three-stripe, the clothing is just so simple and just not unique that if other traders wanted to adopt that to brand or distinguish their own clothes, they should be able to because it's just so simple, like a circle or a triangle."

Was it a deliberate act?

The court case could test the limits of Adidas's trademark. (Supplied)

Dr Hook said in Australia, Adidas's trademark stated a single or two-stripe design would not infringe.

"The fact that [White Fox have] done four stripes seems deliberate because it seems like they've looked at what [Adidas] are covering in the monopoly in the trademark, which is the three stripes, and thinking, 'Well, let's have a look at four stripes,'" she said.

"So maybe this is testing the limits of that."

What does Katy Perry's loss in the High Court mean for her business? Australian fashion designer Katie Perry has won her long-running trademark battle against pop star Katy Perry, but questions about whether the singer will be able to sell her clothing merchandise as part of any future tours remain.

Dr Hopper speculated White Fox may have used the four-stripe design for several reasons.

"One, it was a deliberate act to garner sort of PR.

"Two, they had advice that this is fine; it's not going to be trademark infringement or passing off or breach of the Australian Consumer Law, or they think that there's a pretty good case to be made.

"Thirdly, they had advice that maybe they could revoke the trademarks on which Adidas has sued them."

The case has been set down for a hearing in early 2027.

Adidas and White Fox Boutique have been contacted for comment.

ABC/AAP

title: Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to ditch private health over changes
text:
Nearly 80,000 older Australians are expected to dump their private health cover by the end of the decade as a result of the federal government's controversial proposed changes.

The latest estimate is nearly double the 44,000 figure repeatedly cited by the federal government in defence of the policy.

The proposal would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover, banking about $3 billion to spend elsewhere in the aged care system.

However, health department analysis released under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws reveals that while 44,000 Australians are expected to drop their cover in 2028-29, that is forecast to rise to a cumulative total of 78,000 by the following year.

The Coalition said Health Minister Mark Butler had consistently used the smaller figure to defend the policy.

Anne Ruston says older Australians cannot afford to live without private health insurance. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

"Either he didn't read his own briefs, or he's been deliberately misleading older Australians," Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said.

The health department said the estimate of 44,000 represented the "initial effect of the policy at a point in time" and noted the estimates were subject to uncertainty, as they were based on historical data and responses that might not reflect future behaviour under new policy settings.

Calls for Greens to block legislation

The proposal has come under increasing scrutiny, with the states and territories, aged care advocates and the private health insurance industry all raising concerns about whether the move would heap pressure on the public health system and affect vulnerable older Australians.

The federal government is counting on the $3 billion in expected savings from the changes, having already promised to funnel the money into other major aged care commitments.

Private health changes appear doomed The Greens signal they will not back the government's controversial private health insurance changes as they stand.

However, with the Coalition already vowing to block the legislation in the Senate, the federal government must get the Greens on board for the bill to pass.

The minor party has been playing hardball, declaring last week it would not support the legislation in its current form.

Last month, the ABC revealed about $1.6 billion of the forecast savings would be clawed back from pensioners, according to Parliamentary Budget Office analysis.

Health department figures also revealed that of the more than 3.2 million older Australians affected by the changes, about 2 million live on less than $37,000 a year.

The Greens are now canvassing different options to amend the legislation, such as exempting pensioners from the changes.

Independent MP Monique Ryan called on the Greens to thwart the bill.

"This is a measure which affects pensioners more than any other group, and particularly affects low-income pensioners, so the Greens should come to the table and they should block this measure," Dr Ryan said.

"This is a government which is refusing to be transparent about a really important measure and Australians need to hold them to account."

Outside parliament, health economists including former health department boss Stephen Duckett backed the policy, saying the impact on the public health system would be trivial.

Public policy think tank The Australia Institute also argued the money could be better spent on services that improve health and reduce hospital demand.

Mark Butler announced the changes to private health for older Australians in a pre-budget speech earlier this year. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

A federal government spokesperson said the changes were about "making the private health insurance rebates fairer" and the overall number of people with private health insurance would continue to increase.

"The current additional rebate is simply not the best way to spend precious taxpayers' dollars on behalf of older Australians when we need to do so much heavy lifting in aged care," they said.

"Every dollar will be reinvested to deliver more aged care beds, more packages and better care for older Australians."

Horizon Gold has unleashed a volley of high-grade gold hits from recent drilling at its sprawling 100 per cent-owned Gum Creek project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, headlined by a stunning 44-metre intersection grading 5.08 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. The eye-catching result came from Snook, a prospect highlighted by two historic pits 24.5km north of the Gidgee mill. It returned 11m at a stellar 16.3g/t gold from 174m downhole in the deepest drilling yet at the prospect, with a conga line of impressive intercepts pointing to potential for a much larger open pit and a possible underground operation. A reverse circulation drilling rig at Horizon Gold’s 100 per cent-owned Gum Creek project in Western Australia, where drilling returned 44m at 5.08g/t gold. Other standout results included 14m at 5.18g/t from 88m, featuring an 8-metre zone at 8.81g/t and 12m at 5.72g/t from 135m, including 5m at a solid 10.93g/t. A deeper hit returned 14m at 4.12g/t from 204m, with an impressive three-metre section at 15.33g/t. Heading into the campaign, Snook carried a 54,000-ounce resource defined across 550m of strike and up to 70m wide. The 25-hole, 5151m reverse circulation (RC) program is aiming to push that resource down-plunge to the south. Horizon says the drilling has now confirmed mineralisation to a depth of up to 230m below surface and further defined a steeply south-plunging high-grade system beneath both historic pits.

Although Cobia was previously open-pit mined, the prospect has no current resource. At Alma May - another former open-pit operation 26.5km north of Gidgee with no current resource - 14 holes covering 964m tested shallow ground along strike to the north. Results included 5m at 2.79g/t from 26m, with a one-metre slice at 12.5g/t. Drilling confirmed gold in weathered, quartz-veined rock and room to extend mineralisation north of the pit. Horizon Gold managing director Scott Williamson said: “With follow-up drilling already underway across multiple prospects and further programs planned, we see meaningful scope to enhance project economics well beyond the recent DFS.” Horizon expects to deliver maiden resource estimates for Alma May and Cobia over the coming months, while a resource update is also planned for the high-flying Snook prospect. Once complete, drilling will resume, including diamond work south of the Cobia pit, shallow infill and extension programs, and pit optimisation at Alma May.

Advertisement

The latest results add another layer of intrigue to Horizon’s broader Gum Creek development ambitions, which are built around a substantial gold inventory and an established mining district with a long production history. Gum Creek, 640km northeast of Perth, is a classic brownfields revival story. More than one million ounces have been produced from 37 open pits and three underground mines, while a 110-person camp, operational airstrip and extensive haul roads give Horizon a substantial development head start. Operations ceased in 2005, when gold was languishing at A$560 an ounce. Today’s much stronger gold market gives Horizon a very different launchpad. The company’s July definitive feasibility study (DFS) outlined a robust plan for a new 2.4-million-tonne-a-year processing plant at Gidgee, underpinned by a 728,000-ounce ore reserve. It envisages a 10-year operation producing an average of 88,000 ounces a year, peaking at 114,000 ounces in year two and recovering 880,000 ounces over the mine life. It forecasts pre-production capital of A$350M and an all-in sustaining cost of A$2,995 an ounce. The real kicker is that this starter case draws on only a fraction of Gum Creek’s global resource of 37.97 million tonnes grading 1.89g/t for 2.3 million ounces of gold. A 416,000-ounce free-milling underground resource and the 400,000-ounce Wilsons sulphide deposit also sit outside the current mine plan, offering further growth beyond the DFS case.

Advertisement

Snook, Cobia and Alma May are similarly excluded from the initial mine plan, so success across the three prospects could add significant scale to the project’s already substantial gold inventory. Alongside its work, Horizon is targeting a final investment decision on the company’s main Gum Creek development in the second quarter of 2027, with first gold targeted in the second half of 2028. Horizon has a solid DFS in its back pocket and high-grade hits emerging beyond the initial mine plan at Cobia, Alma May and Snook. The new resource estimates could add further weight to the growth story, showing the DFS may be just the floor, not the ceiling. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Josh Frydenberg has criticised the direction of the Liberal Party, arguing it must change in the face of an existential threat. The former treasurer, who was considered a future Liberal leader before losing his seat in 2022, has stoked speculation he will run again with the release of a new memoir, which includes criticism the party has lost touch with its roots, as well as his proposals for policy remedies. Former treasurer Josh Frydenberg has left the door open to a political comeback. Eddie Jim The intervention creates a fresh headache for Taylor, who immediately shut down Frydenberg’s suggestion that a Coalition government should raise the GST to offset income and business tax cuts. Taylor returned to parliament this week after addressing the annual Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane on Saturday, where he was heckled by One Nation loyalists in the audience and ridiculed by the next speaker, Pauline Hanson.

Advertisement

On Sunday night, Frydenberg said Taylor was copping criticism from “lots of corners” by people saying the party needed to do better. “The polls are showing that the Liberal Party is at an all-time low,” Frydenberg told 60 Minutes. “And so, things have to change. Because there’s something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces.” Treasurer Jim Chalmers exploited Frydenberg’s criticism of the party’s direction during question time to mock Taylor. Chalmers took a Dorothy Dixer about Labor’s economic management when he turned to the debt left after Frydenberg’s time in government, and the former member for Kooyong’s latest pitch to lift the GST. “The leader of the opposition (Angus Taylor) is being stalked from the inside by the member for Canning (Andrew Hastie). He’s being stalked from the outside by the failed former member for Kooyong (Frydenberg),” Chalmers said.

Advertisement

Chalmers said shadow treasurer Tim Wilson had also floated increasing the GST to 20 per cent in his first speech to parliament. Taylor quickly nixed the suggestion on Sunday when asked about Frydenberg’s proposal. Frydenberg has denied his book was a pitch for the prime ministership, but when asked if he still had aspirations to lead the country, said he had not closed that door. “I don’t need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away,” he said. A political comeback for the former treasurer would involve a protracted campaign for a seat with weak preference flows that the Liberals failed to recapture in 2025. He would also have to win a preselection contest, which some senior Victorian Liberal operatives unsupportive of Frydenberg want resolved by the first quarter of next year. But Frydenberg’s supporters suggest he will seek to delay an announcement on his candidacy until the latest possible moment, as he assesses the political terrain and the likelihood of winning the seat.

Advertisement

The Coalition is trailing Labor and One Nation in the polls, and Taylor is behind Anthony Albanese and Pauline Hanson as preferred prime minister, though he edged up 1 point in the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson, who in 2025 became the first Liberal to reclaim a seat from a teal independent, said on Monday he had no issue with Frydenberg putting himself forward at the next election. “I think it’s always good to have candidates who want to step up and run and make sure we pick up seats so that Angus Taylor can be prime minister of this country,” Wilson told Radio National. Fellow Coalition frontbenchers Andrew Bragg and Angie Bell, who Frydenberg reveals in his book were part of a meeting of moderates in 2021 to discuss concerns about then prime minister Scott Morrison’s leadership, have urged the former treasurer to run.

Advertisement

In the 60 Minutes interview, Frydenberg said he stood by his decision not to challenge Morrison for the leadership at that time. “During my time in office, there were numerous changes of prime ministership and leadership of the Liberal Party, and in each time, I stood by the incumbent, and I don’t regret that,” he said. Frydenberg said he was more disappointed by the multiple ministries scandal, in which Morrison secretly swore himself into the portfolios of several colleagues, including Frydenberg’s. Related Article Political leadership Monique Ryan says Frydenberg focused on the past, amid accusations of a ‘toxic’ campaign “I was angry about it, and I felt undermined. It was completely unnecessary for him to do that, and I think a lot of colleagues felt blindsided,” he said.

Advertisement

“I made it very clear that it was unnecessary, and he said to me that he would have made the same decision again, and I said you can’t be serious. So that’s something that he’ll obviously have to explain for himself. But it has damaged our relationship.” Current Kooyong MP, independent Monique Ryan, on Monday said she was not bothered who the Liberal Party put up as a candidate at the next election. She added that Frydenberg had his chance with voters. Independent MP Monique Ryan said Kooyong had already rejected Frydenberg. Luis Enrique Ascui “He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change,” Ryan told Seven’s Sunrise. “People were unhappy with his economic management. People were very unhappy with the way that he punched down on Victoria during the COVID years. I’m not sure what has changed since that time that Mr Frydenberg now thinks that the community will welcome him back with open arms.”

She accused Frydenberg of being too focused on ongoing prime ministerial ambitions instead of his community. “He doesn’t speak much about Kooyong, and that’s the part of the world that I’m most focused on.” After initially avoiding Frydenberg’s claims last week that her supporters had run a campaign rife with personal abuse, Ryan said on Monday she rejected that characterisation. “It does not match with my own recollections or the recollections of the more than 2000 people who volunteered with me. We know that we conducted a campaign run with integrity and in a good spirit,” she told reporters in Canberra. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. As Victorians start to lock in to the choice before them at next month’s state election, the political contest is being fought overwhelmingly on the Coalition’s preferred ground, with the economy, financial management and crime the dominant issues on voters’ minds. The latest Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead shows that Premier Ben Carroll’s personal popularity has taken a 9-point dive to minus 11, suggesting voters have weighed up Labor’s newest leader and aren’t convinced by what they see. Premier Ben Carroll is being dogged by a new problem – sinking personal popularity. Jason South Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, by contrast, has established herself as one of Australia’s most popular political leaders, with her already strong personal likeability climbing 4 percentage points to 23. Voting intentions are little changed since last month’s Resolve poll, with Labor stuck on primary support of 25 per cent, the Coalition unmoved on 28 and One Nation steady on 23 per cent.

Advertisement

While these numbers, if replicated on November 28, would almost certainly deliver a change of government, it is less clear whether the Coalition would be able to form a majority government without the help of One Nation or another minor party. The only significant movers in this latest poll are the Victorian Greens, who for the first time in three years are showing signs of electoral growth with a 3-point boost to their primary support. This has come at the expense of independents, who attracted support from only 4 per cent of the 1000 respondents surveyed. If replicated on election day, this could deliver stronger preference flows to Labor in some seats. Early polling in Victoria opens in just over six weeks.

Advertisement

Resolve founder Jim Reed said one of the key findings of the survey was that people were now paying closer attention. “Fewer and fewer voters are telling us they are uncommitted each month, and the number of people undecided on their preferred leader is also dropping, which is evidence that they are starting to pay attention and lock in,” he said. “Victorians were willing to give Carroll a fair go, but after a few months they are increasingly unconvinced. His net likeability and preferred premier metrics are both down. And Wilson is benefiting from that.” The most encouraging news for the Coalition from this survey, other than the level of personal support for Wilson, is that its areas of perceived relative strength – economic and financial management, and crime and policing – are at the top of voters’ priority lists.

Advertisement

When asked what their highest priority issue was for deciding how to vote, 33 per cent of respondents nominated the state’s economy and finances, while 24 per cent said crime and policing. The second-highest priority – the traditional Labor strength of hospitals and health services – was nominated by 12 per cent of respondents. When asked to nominate things that will most influence their vote from a list of more specific issues and policy announcements, 27 per cent chose government spending and debt, while 21 per cent went for youth crime. Greens voters nominated artificial intelligence and data centres as their biggest vote-shaping concern. The survey was conducted between October 6 and October 10, in the aftermath of One Nation’s Victorian policy and campaign launch, which featured a grab bag of uncosted promises.

Advertisement

The boldest policy announcement of the week was Jess Wilson’s $1.27 billion promise to halve the elective surgery waiting list by booking 25,000 additional patients into private hospitals to have surgery on the public tab. This masthead on Monday revealed the policy involved bringing forward $1.1 billion of borrowed money earmarked for future capital investment over the next decade to cover the cost of the urgent surgeries. Previously unpublished budget figures show the opposition’s accounting would create an $880 million shortfall in its election costings. Carroll leapt on the revelation on Monday, telling 3AW, “The opposition leader says she knows everything and can do both treasury and leader. That has now seen a billion-dollar budget black hole in her costings on health.” Wilson defended the credibility of her costings by saying she would not be “lectured by the Labor Party on economic mismanagement in this state”.

Advertisement

“Budgets don’t just look at one policy in isolation. They don’t just look at the spend of one policy in isolation. They look at policies – that’s both savings and expenditure – in aggregate over those four years, taking into account the net debt position, looking at the forecast, and of course, the operating position in the state,” Wilson said. She repeated her goal of returning the state’s finances to cash surplus by 2032 if elected in November, and said it was only at this point – when the state is raising more in revenue than it spends on operating expenses and capital investments – that reducing net debt becomes possible. Jess Wilson, pictured with Nationals leader Danny O’Brien, has defended the costings behind her policy for public patients to access elective surgery through private hospitals. Luis Enrique Ascui Reed said the electoral challenge before the Coalition – to gain an additional 16 seats required to form majority government – remained a big ask, but noted the dominant issues and the respective likeability of the leaders are pointing in the right direction for the Liberal and National parties. “Things like potholes and the Suburban Rail Loop are handy icons for voters to talk about, but our polling is telling us that the foundational issues of economic health, debt and crime are what’s driving votes,” Reed said. “This is Coalition ground.”

title: The Wallabies have faced the music. Can they now change their Bledisloe tune?
text:

Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The Wallabies have faced the music. Can they now change their Bledisloe tune? Monday press conferences after a Bledisloe Cup defeat would have to rank among the least appealing assignments for any Wallabies player. Particularly when Saturday’s 50-19 capitulation against the All Blacks at Eden Park marked Australia’s 12th consecutive defeat to their trans-Tasman rivals. Loading On the second floor of a hotel across the road from Accor Stadium at Sydney Olympic Park, the venue for Saturday’s dead-rubber Bledisloe clash, Wallabies fullback Tom Wright was the one chosen to explain how Australia had conceded so many points. “The guys were obviously really disappointed with the result,” Wright said. “The group came together on Sunday morning [to] face the music.”

Advertisement

Face the music? From coaches? Or senior players laying down the law? “The music of the scoreboard,” Wright said. “No one wants to be on the receiving end of 50 points. No one wants to be on the receiving end of a loss. At 17-14 [in front], we’re right in the contest, and the game was there to be taken. We knew the opportunity was there for us. Tom Wright of Australia reacts to the loss. Getty Images “We felt like all the guns were loaded, and we had the ammunition to fire shots and win the game. We didn’t. That’s the music that we’re talking about. You can be internally so driven to win and when you don’t … that’s the disappointment you’ve got to face.” For all the optimism generated by a six-game unbeaten streak before last weekend, including a surprise win over the Springboks, the broader Australian sporting public ultimately judges the Wallabies on one thing: whether they can beat the All Blacks.

Advertisement

And when it comes to New Zealand, the same old problems keep resurfacing. Some would have turned on the television expecting a spirited second-half performance, but all they got was a botched Australian lineout deep in Kiwi territory that became the catalyst for an All Blacks onslaught that turned a contest into another humiliating defeat. It was a familiar script, even if the Wallabies had spent much of the first half threatening to rewrite it. The aerial contest wasn’t a contest. Inevitably, out came the same questions that get rolled out every year. What is it about the All Blacks? Is there a mental inferiority complex when it comes to Eden Park?

Advertisement

Wright, one of Australia’s best on Saturday after scoring the opening try on Saturday, is not one for magic solutions. “If I had the golden egg answer, it’d be pretty handy,” Wright said. “But I certainly don’t think there are any mental scars. Wallabies head coach Les Kiss. Getty Images “They’re not a poor team. The narrative will always be that ... we haven’t got our hands on the Bledisloe Cup, and we haven’t got a win against them [in 12 attempts]. “We know that the Bledisloe Cup remains across the ditch. We can’t carry that disappointment into the rest of this week because it’s not going to help us win on Saturday, is it?”

Advertisement

Former Wallaby Tim Horan spoke for plenty of frustrated Australian supporters on Sunday when asked on Channel Nine about the familiar narrative that the Wallabies would “learn” from their mistakes across the ditch. “I just don’t like hearing, ‘oh we’re going to learn from this’. I think Aussies are sick of getting beaten by the All Blacks,” Horan said. Loading Add Wright to that list. But for the doom and gloom around Australia’s inability to reclaim the Bledisloe Cup, a drought now stretching 24 years, the Wallabies have promised themselves they won’t spend the week feeling sorry for themselves.

Advertisement

The trophy is gone for another year, but Saturday presents an opportunity to restore some pride and avoid a clean sweep. Related Article Australian rugby Box clever: Wallabies say accuracy and urgency keys to combatting All Blacks’ aerial dominance Australia and New Zealand also face each other in the pool stages at next year’s Rugby World Cup at the same venue. There will be an element of wanting to land an early psychological blow ahead of a game that really matters. “You can be disappointed, but you’ve got to pick up the pieces pretty quickly to be able to move on and give ourselves a good opportunity this Saturday,” Wright said. “The guys are pretty keen to get back on the horse.”

Advertisement

One player unavailable for the Wallabies’ final match before their European spring tour is Jordan Petaia, who missed the Auckland clash after suffering a syndesmosis injury at training last week. Petaia is expected to be sidelined for about a month after being caught in an awkward tackle involving several Wallabies players, including Max Jorgensen, in the lead-up to the first Bledisloe Test.

title: They’ve been a lost cause for 10 years. The Wanderers may have finally worked out why
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerA-League Men They’ve been a lost cause for 10 years. The Wanderers may have finally worked out why Vince Rugari October 12, 2026 — 3:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. As an actor, Ufuk Talay makes a very good football coach. The new Western Sydney Wanderers boss is the frontman of a cheeky commercial for the A-League club’s sponsor, property management group Starr Partners, in which he pokes fun at his controversial defection from arch-rivals Sydney FC, setting the tone for a spicy season-opening derby on Friday night. View post on X It’s filled with unsubtle Easter eggs - Talay replacing sky blue things with red and black, nods to famous footballing turncoats such as Luis Figo and Sol Campbell - and ends with Milos Ninkovic, the most high-profile player to have switched from Sydney to the Wanderers, welcoming him to the neighbourhood. It’s also the hardest thing Talay reckons he’s ever done.

Advertisement

“I’m not an actor, I’ll tell you that much,” he laughed. “It was actually quite enjoyable, but very stressful at the same time. I did so many takes … they’d go, ‘That was excellent, but can you just smile at the end, please?’ I’m just trying to remember the line, not remember about smiling. New Wanderers football director Mal Impiombato and coach Ufuk Talay at the club’s Rooty Hill base. James Brickwood “Overall, I think it was good fun. I think it adds a bit of banter to the derby that we play in the first round.” It remains to be seen how Talay is received by Sydney fans at Allianz Stadium, which is tracking for a crowd of over 35,000. Many of them were happy to see the back of Talay anyway, and have since embraced the club’s new direction under Patrick Kisnorbo.

Advertisement

The Wanderers faithful, meanwhile, are daring to dream again after a productive off-season, in which they went unbeaten in trial matches against A-League opposition (they were knocked out of the Australia Cup on penalties by Melbourne Victory) and suffered their only defeat to visiting Chelsea, of all teams. Their squad looks decent enough, but then again, that’s never really been the problem. The only defeat the Wanderers have tasted in regulation time this pre-season was against Chelsea. Getty With all due respect to Talay, the club’s ninth coach since the departure of inaugural boss Tony Popovic, in which time they’ve played finals only twice, he is not the most important appointment the Wanderers have made. Finally, they have addressed a key off-field vacuum above the coach and filled it with one of the game’s most respected operators.

Advertisement

Step forward, Mal Impiombato, the club’s inaugural director of football. His name may not resonate widely, but his track record suggests he could be exactly what the Wanderers need. Ufuk Talay during his days at Sydney FC. Getty Images Out of a job after the collapse of Western United, having essentially served as the architect of the defunct club’s productive football department, Impiombato has spent the last few months trying to understand why one of Australian football’s biggest clubs has been punching below its weight for so long. His diagnosis was as straightforward as his proposed remedy, and it will not shock anyone: the Wanderers had the resources, facilities and talent, but their various football departments were operating in isolation, without a coherent strategy to connect them.

Advertisement

Since arriving in April, Impiombato has tried to bring their men’s, women’s, academy and even disability programs closer together, establishing clearer lines of communication and responsibility, as well as a common set of playing principles which will govern how any Wanderers team tries to approach any game, the profile of players who are brought into the club, and what kind of players they develop internally. “People think you’re going to add this whole new plethora of things that no one’s ever heard of before,” said Impiombato, who has also worked at two other A-League clubs as well as Football Australia. Ufuk Talay in the dugout for Sydney FC. Getty “There’s no groundbreaking thing that I wanted to bring in, outside of the fundamental basics of what makes teams successful, and that’s stability, structure and a bit of strategic direction and alignment to understand where we want to go and how we want to get there.” It’s boring, but hopefully, the outcomes won’t be.

Advertisement

If it wasn’t clear enough from the ad he fronted, Talay knows that the life of a coach is transient and insecure. The work done by Impiombato is intended to ensure that the Wanderers’ own identity is far less reliant on the identity of their coach, which is how Talay reckons it should be. “As much as I’m the coach of the team, I still believe that it should be a club-centred model, not a coach-centred model,” Talay said. “The coach comes in, and he goes, ‘No, no, we’ll scrap everything that you’ve done for the last year, the last five years, and we’ll restart and do it again.’ And I don’t think that actually works.” Even better for Talay, the presence of Impiombato provides him with something few of his predecessors have enjoyed: a layer of protection from chairman Paul Lederer and his board if results take a turn for the worse and their trigger fingers get itchy. “Having a football director that sits above me, between me and the board, gives me a buffer,” he said. “It’s very important to have a person like Mal, who’s a fantastic human being first and foremost. He’s the guy that will hopefully protect me when things aren’t going as well so that there’s no knee-jerk decisions, emotional decisions … it allows me to focus on my job.”

Advertisement

Of course, none of this guarantees success, and Wanderers fans have heard it all before. The past decade has been filled with false dawns, and Talay is the first to admit that their impressive pre-season results will be meaningless if they don’t show the same stuff when there are points on the line. Related Article Analysis

Australia Cup Let them in: South Melbourne just showed the A-League what it has been missing The real test begins on Friday night against the club Talay left behind, in front of a crowd that will be eager to see him fail. On his end, at least, there are no hard feelings. “Players make changes, coaches make changes. For me, home is where you’re at,” Talay said.

Advertisement

“This is what I do as a job to look after my family. The reality is I’m at Western Sydney at the moment, I’m very happy to be here, and I’ll do everything possible to help the group and help the club move forward, and hopefully bring some sort of success. “In a few years’ time, that might change again, and you’re somewhere else. That’s the nature of our game. You put your hat down and be ready to pick it up and move on to the next thing.” When that day comes, at least he’ll know which company to call.

Logging from a new drillhole 1.25 kilometres from its recent high-grade gold discovery has revealed a 34-metre-wide zone of alteration and quartz veining from just 62m downhole. The company says the geology in the new hole is visually similar to the earlier discovery hole that returned a stellar 18m at 7.31 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. The interval includes sections of stronger quartz-sulphide veining and visually estimated pyrite of up to an impressive 0.8 per cent. Dalaroo Metals’ geos inspecting reverse circulation chip trays for mineralisation at its Bondoukou high-grade gold discovery in Côte d’Ivoire. The new visual results build on a spectacular maiden drilling campaign that recently delivered the headline hit of 18m at 7.31g/t gold from 63m in just the second hole drilled. Notably, that discovery hole also included a second, deeper zone of 16m grading 1.46g/t gold from 113m, along with an initial hole that landed a solid 23-metre intercept running 2.14g/t gold right from surface. Samples from the new hole are in transit and have been prioritised for a fast turnaround, with results expected before the end of this month. Assays for the previous holes drilled in the campaign are also at the laboratory, with results anticipated from early November.

′ Our focus is on building the geological evidence to assess the scale and continuity of the mineralisation.′ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan The ongoing work forms part of Dalaroo’s maiden 24-hole, 4200-metre orientation program, the opening salvo in a much bigger 12,000-metre reverse circulation (RC) program targeting the Wilfred, Mag and Ali prospects at Bondoukou. So far, the company has completed 10 RC holes, totalling 2252m, across its Wilfred prospect. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “Our first reported high-grade gold intersections at Wilfred established an exciting starting point for exploration at Gold Ridge. We are encouraged that hole has now encountered alteration, quartz-sulphide veining and a rock sequence comparable to that seen in the discovery hole. The immediate priority is to establish, through laboratory assays and follow-up drilling, whether these geological features are associated with further gold mineralisation and how the system is oriented.” The new hole was drilled north-west of the company’s original discovery holes along the interpreted 7km-long Gold Ridge corridor. Both holes intersected a similar package of rocks at broadly similar depths, despite being drilled more than a kilometre apart and in opposite directions. Dalaroo believes this apparent geological link-up could strongly indicate the scale of the mineralising system it has on its hands. The company is certainly not standing still, with the RC rig now setting up for a scissor hole, designed to intersect the new 34-metre alteration zone at depth and at a different angle to help define its orientation. After completing work at Wilfred, the rig will move on to test the nearby Ali and Mag prospects.

In parallel, a diamond drill rig is scheduled to mobilise to the project in mid-to-late October to begin follow-up work around the original high-grade discovery. The company is also finalising plans for an induced polarisation geophysics survey along the entire 7km-long Gold Ridge corridor to help prioritise additional drill targets. The Bondoukou project lies in the prolific Birimian greenstone belt, a rapidly emerging gold district just 35 kilometres from Endeavour Mining’s giant five-million-ounce Tanda-Iguela gold project. The belt also hosts a string of other multi-million-ounce gold deposits, making it one of Africa’s most well-endowed gold regions. While West Africa is the clear focus, Dalaroo is also advancing other projects in its portfolio. At its Blue Lagoon project in Greenland, the company is chasing rare earths, while closer to home, an induced-polarisation survey has firmed up several compelling drill targets at its Watheroo copper-nickel-PGE project in WA. After making a high-grade discovery with some of its earliest drill holes at Bondoukou, Dalaroo now has visual evidence that the system could extend for some distance. With a bevvy of assays due in the coming weeks and a suite of exploration activities kicking off, the market will likely be watching closely to see just how big this West African gold play could be. WA Premier Roger Cook says WA’s universities could sell land for housing to help fund a proposed three-way merger between Curtin, Murdoch and the University of Western Australia. Opposition to the merger has heated up after the WA government announced it would develop a business case to see whether a mega-university stacked up. More than two-thirds of university staff surveyed opposed the proposal Curtin University vice chancellor Harlene Hayne and the WA opposition have pointed to job losses and the blown out costs of the Adelaide University merger, which has reached more than $1 billion. The National Tertiary Education Union also released survey results in Monday that found 68.7 per cent of the 936 university staff surveyed opposed the proposal.

Advertisement

Cook sought to allay fears that taxpayers would be on the line for the merger costs by suggesting the universities could sell land. “We believe this should be not up to the WA taxpayer to foot all the bill,” he said. “They’ve got significant parcels of land, land which could be repurposed for housing, and so that’s an explicit objective of the steering committee.” He rejected opposition concerns the merger could cost the state between $1 billion to $2 billion. “By critics of the proposal, yes, it has [been estimated to coast $1 billion], but we have an explicit objective of the steering committee who are putting together the business case for this to be self-funding,” he said.

Advertisement

Related Article University Battle lines drawn as Curtin opposes WA’s mega-university plan The business case comes after two separate reports into the sector in 2023 and 2025 that called for a merger to create a more competitive university globally. Cook said the three-way merger was “preordained”. “We’ll look at the business case. If it stacks up, well, then obviously we’ll take the opportunities that come with it,” he said. “I believe this is an important reform. It’s important to make sure we have a world-class university from Western Australia, not only for our students, but for our economy.”

Advertisement

According to the union survey results, opposition to the merger was strongest at Curtin University at 75 per cent. Those opposed pointed to the disruption that followed the Adelaide University merger, the scale of likely job losses, and the size and complexity of the merged university. The tertiary union will be part of the steering committee and Curtin branch president Professor Scott Fitzgerald said he would be relaying the opposition. “That’s exactly the message I’ll be delivering as part of the steering committee. Beyond that, we’ll be using everything at our disposal to fight hard against a merger,” he said. “It’s highly concerning that the committee’s work is centred on a business case. Public universities exist to serve students, staff and the wider community. Any decision about their future should be through that focus, not a simplistic approach that puts profits over people.”

Advertisement

Murdoch University urged the state government to re-consider the merger in a statement released on Sunday. “The potential merger is at odds with the federal government’s approach to higher education policy as expressed through the Australian Universities Accord and the establishment of the Australian Tertiary Education Commission, which promotes a greater diversity of universities across Australia,” a spokeswoman said. “As we have stated continually throughout the merger debate, we believe Western Australia is best served by having four public universities, each with its own special characteristics.” The steering committee will be led by Fortescue deputy chair Mark Barnaba and medical researcher Professor Fiona Wood as deputy chair.

title: Josh Frydenberg says 'things have to change' as he questions Liberal leadership
text:
In brief Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg has criticised Angus Taylor's leadership of the Liberal Party.

He told Nine's 60 Minutes that 'things have to change' after Liberal polling fell to an all-time low.

Angus Taylor would welcome the political return of Josh Frydenberg to parliament, despite the former treasurer attacking his leadership of the Liberal Party.

Frydenberg used an interview to criticise Taylor's handling of the party, saying the current leader had contributed to Liberal polling being at an "all-time low".

"Things have to change, because there's something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces," he told Nine's 60 Minutes on Sunday night.

"[Taylor is] getting [criticism] from lots of corners. People are saying that the Liberal Party needs to do better."

The latest Newspoll had the Coalition's primary support at 20 per cent, compared to Labor's 29 per cent and One Nation's 26 per cent.

Excerpts from Frydenberg's memoir, which is likely to contain policy suggestions, have fuelled rumours that he is planning to make a political comeback.

"Look, I certainly haven't closed the door, but I don't need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away," he said.

Despite the criticism, Taylor said his former Liberal colleague would be welcomed back into the fold should he decide to run.

The Liberal Party's fortunes have not improved after Angus Taylor took over as leader in February. Source: AAP / Bianca de Marchi

"I welcome every Liberal who cares about the future of our nation — and I know Josh does — to put shoulder to the wheel in the coming months to get rid of a rotten Labor government and make the change that Australia needs happen," he told reporters in Canberra on Monday.

"I ask all Liberals and Nationals and people who are supportive of our view about where the country needs to go … to get in there and help in any way they can."

Frydenberg held the Melbourne seat of Kooyong for 12 years from 2010 and was treasurer in the Morrison government, including through the COVID-19 pandemic.

He lost the seat to independent MP Monique Ryan at the 2022 election, in which she won almost 53 per cent of the two-party preferred vote.

Ryan appeared unfazed by her competition's possible return.

"I'm not bothered either way," she told Nine's Today program.

"Josh does have a track record with the Kooyong community."

"He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change.

"People were unhappy with his economic management."

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson has encouraged others to put themselves forward as Liberal candidates. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson encouraged people to "put themselves forward" as candidates to create a stronger Liberal Party.

"I encourage them to do so, so they can be part of a winning team. So we can have an Angus Taylor-led government," he told ABC Radio.

"What we need is people who've got courage in their hearts and are prepared to make the sacrifices necessary for public office."

title: Should you be paid to exercise while at work? These Australian researchers think so
text:
IN BRIEF: Physical inactivity costs the Australian economy $2 billion annually, the Heart Research Institute says.

Researchers believe the introduction of exercise while at work could have significant health outcomes.

Should workers get paid exercise breaks? It's a question Australian researchers are asking in an upcoming trial, as they track health outcomes and productivity for shift workers given time to exercise on the job.

Researchers believe targeted measures to address physical inactivity could improve Australia's cardiovascular health, mental health, and physical wellbeing.

Heart disease is a key health issue in Australia, with more than one million Australians aged 18 and over (6.4 per cent of the adult population) living with one or more conditions related to heart, stroke or vascular disease in 2024, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

Regular exercise can reduce the risk of heart disease by up to a third, while helping to lower blood pressure, improve cholesterol levels, and strengthen the heart muscle.

The Heart Research Institute says physical inactivity costs the Australian economy over $2 billion annually.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Cardiologist Dr Faraz Pathan says physical inactivity is a "costly exercise", and that scale-able solutions are needed.

Physical inactivity "leads to a burden of cardiovascular disease and mental health issues", he said, and the increased risk of developing cancers.

"That means we lose staff to absenteeism. We lose people to illnesses. We lose people to the premature truncation of their careers," he told SBS News.

"Amplified at the level of society and economy, this is a very costly exercise."

Dr Faraz Pathan (centre) says scale-able solutions are needed for physical inactivity. Source: SBS News

For nurse Lisa Barry, who has three children, exercise fell down the priority list as life got busier.

"You get home from work absolutely exhausted, and the last thing you feel like doing is exercising," she told SBS News.

"So having it as part of your workday would be fantastic."

Lisa is one of 100 healthcare workers at Nepean Hospital in Western Sydney who will be given 30-minute exercise breaks during their shifts for the upcoming study, with activities including walking, boxing, and virtual reality tennis.

'The intervention is not actually exercise'

The trial, led by the Heart Research Institute, is set to begin next year.

"The intervention is not actually exercise," Pathan said.

"It is the time, the opportunity in your workday to exercise, so you get back home, you can be a mum or a dad, look after your elderly parents."

Pathan says having hospital shift workers as study participants presents unique challenges that researchers will be looking to tackle.

"Why a hospital? Because I think shift work is a significant cardiometabolic risk factor — we have a large proportion of shift workers — but so is physical inactivity, so is chronic stress.

"I do think doing a trial like this in hospital is doing it on hard mode, because there are competing priorities.

"But if we can pull it off in this group, and if we show that people are doing better, well then I would love to see this implemented in businesses and in environments across Australia.

"My dream is for Australia to be the first country that brings this into existence for workers.

'We've led the world in public policy before, so I think we can be ambitious."

The 12-month study aims to examine whether exercising on the clock improves staff cardiovascular health.

Researchers will compare the results of participants who were given exercise breaks at the start of the 12 months with those who receive them 6 months later.

Researchers looking for broader wellbeing benefits

Pathan says the study will track changes in heart health and fitness, but that researchers will carefully look for any differences in overall wellbeing, including mental health.

"Is depression improved? Is burnout improved? Is anxiety improved?

"Because I think some of the benefit may not only be cardiovascular. It may actually be in your mental health and wellbeing as well."

Pathan believes small amounts of exercise built into the working day can make a huge difference over time, and if the study is successful, he said he hopes the idea could be rolled out to workplaces around the country.

READ MORE A key unknown remains in the government's private health rebate overhaul

Lisa Barry says exercise breaks could improve her energy levels and productivity.

"I think it'll be good for a mental reset," she said.

"And then you come back, and you're ready to go, you're hyped up, you're ready to keep on going with your shift.

"I think it'll have that effect of 'let's finish this shift, let's get through the day'."

title: 'You better think again': Hanson names Liberal leader she'd prefer over 'smarmy' Taylor
text:
IN BRIEF Yesterday, Hanson said the Opposition leader and another Liberal leadership hopeful were unfit to lead the party.

On Saturday, she said Angus Taylor was a "smarmy management consultant" and Tim Wilson was "full of himself".

One Nation's Pauline Hanson has revealed her pick to head right-wing counterparts the Liberals after dismissing its current leader as a "smarmy management consultant".

Angus Taylor became the first sitting Opposition leader to address the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane on Saturday as the Coalition and One Nation vied for the fractured right-wing vote.

But Hanson emerged the crowd favourite as she made jibes about her conservative rivals while also offering to "put personal history aside" and team up with the Coalition to remove Labor from government.

Opposition frontbenchers headlined on Sunday as their leaders swapped the conference stage for the morning media rounds.

Hanson said she did not "want to be around the table" with the Liberals, but they should still work together to get rid of Labor as it would be extremely hard for either One Nation or the Coalition to govern alone.

A day after suggesting Taylor — a former partner at global consulting firm McKinsey & Company — was a "smarmy management consultant", she also dismissed treasury spokesperson and Liberal leadership hopeful Tim Wilson as "full of himself" and "woke".

"He put us last in the last election, called us a racist party," she told News24.

"If they're thinking about Tim Wilson, I think you better think again because I've got no time for that man."

Hanson said she got on "reasonably well" with former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg, who is reportedly mulling a return to politics after losing his seat at the 2022 election.

But she said former prime minister and current party president Tony Abbott was the person with the best chance of leading the Liberals.

Abbott lost his federal seat at the 2019 federal election, when he was defeated by independent candidate Zali Steggall, meaning he'd need to make a return to Canberra to lead the parliamentary wing of the party.

Taylor said he would welcome Frydenberg "playing whatever role he's able to play" as he needed "every good Liberal with [a] shoulder to the wheel" in the lead-up to the next election.

But he poured cold water on an idea floated by the former treasurer to raise the Goods and Services Tax (GST) while lowering income taxes.

"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis ... we'll put Australia and Australians first, but we won't be raising taxes," he told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday.

In an extract from his soon-to-be-published memoir, Frydenberg called on the Coalition to ignore calls to appeal to the extremes and instead target the electoral centre.

But during his speech to the conservative conference, Taylor described the Coalition under his leadership alongside the Nationals' Matt Canavan as "unashamedly on the right".

Opposition energy spokesperson Dan Tehan took the stage on Sunday, telling the audience the Coalition would axe Labor's policies to achieve net-zero emissions.
