title: Coalition defends migration cuts on economic grounds, rejects One Nation-style bans
text:
In Brief Coalition says cutting migration to 100,000 would lift productivity by prioritising higher-skilled workers.

Taylor rejected One Nation-style country bans, saying migrants should be judged on conduct and character.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's proposed migration overhaul as an economic reform designed to boost productivity, while rejecting the idea of banning migrants based on their country of origin.

The Coalition's plan would cut net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000, about a third of current levels, while increasing the share of "high-value" migrants entering Australia.

They have called it the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history".

However, Taylor's comments to ABC's Insiders on Sunday also appeared to mark a shift in tone from his last appearance on the show.

This time, he repeatedly framed the changes as an economic measure aimed at boosting productivity and competitiveness, rather than focusing on national security or cultural concerns.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taylor highlights migration plan as economic reform

Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.

"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.

"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.

"It will raise productivity, it will raise competitiveness, it will raise the average income of the people coming into this city."

Taylor said the policy would increase the average skill level of migrants entering Australia while reducing overall numbers through changes to a range of visa programs, including student, graduate and bridging visas.

He repeatedly argued migration settings should be geared towards lifting productivity rather than simply increasing population growth.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone," he said.

Bringing in more highly skilled migrants would put downward pressure on inflation because it would raise productivity, Taylor argued, saying "this is pretty simple economics".

The Coalition plans to dramatically cut temporary visa holders under their proposed migration policy. Source: SBS News

"When you bring someone to Australia, you are bringing demand and supply. If that person is low-skilled, you are bringing more demand than supply. If they are high-skilled, you are bringing the opposite, actually bringing more supply.

"One of the reasons why we've had a collapse in productivity in this country ... is that our immigration program has not been working to drive up our productivity and it should be."

He also defended the Coalition's proposal to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places, saying "charity begins at home" and such measures were designed to "balance the budget".

Taylor distances Coalition from One Nation approach

While much of Taylor's defence of the policy focused on economics, he also sought to draw a distinction between the Coalition's approach and proposals advanced by One Nation.

The comments marked a different emphasis from Taylor's previous appearance on the same program in April, when he argued migrants from "bad countries" posed a higher risk to Australia.

Pressed at the time on which countries he considered "bad", Taylor pointed to Iran and referred to security concerns involving people arriving from Gaza.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Asked on Sunday why the Coalition had not gone as far as One Nation in proposing immigration restrictions based on nationality, Taylor rejected the comparison.

"I've always said we will discriminate not based on the country someone comes from or their race or their religion, but based on the person and whether that person is a suitable person to be a resident or citizen of this country," he said.

"That's what we should focus on, and we should judge people on their character and conduct, not the colour of their skin."

Taylor maintained that some countries could present higher risks for security agencies to assess.

"It is true that risks are higher where there is a bad regime — there is no question about that."

"That doesn't mean screen them all out. That means make sure you are assessing those risks appropriately."

One Nation has previously proposed measures targeting migration from specific countries, including pausing new migration from countries subject to a federal government 'do not travel' warning.

However, Taylor also linked the Coalition's migration policy to a broader focus on screening prospective visa holders.

"People who do not believe in our system of law, people who do not believe in our basic freedoms, they shouldn't be coming to this country," he said.

"If they've got here on a visa, they should be thrown out."

Later on Sunday, other Coalition figures reiterated those sentiments, following reports that the flydubai co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flight bound for Israel was allegedly radicalised while studying in Melbourne.

Opposition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam said there was no place for "hate preachers who spread extremism, glorify terrorism or encourage violence".

"That is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism," he said.

“At a federal level, we also need stronger visa screening, better intelligence sharing and properly resourced counter-terrorism agencies. That is why the Coalition has committed to establishing an Enhanced Screening Coordination Centre to bring together our intelligence, policing and border protection capabilities."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Australia had its toughest-ever powers to prevent violent extremists entering the country.

"I've been using them to be able to scan and assess whether someone has a history of being a problem before we give them a visa, and we've been cancelling visas when people are here, and we've been stopping people from coming here in the first place," he told News24 on Sunday.

The economic debate over immigration levels

Taylor's argument rests on the idea that a smaller, more highly skilled migration intake would boost productivity while reducing pressure on housing and infrastructure.

However, the economic impacts of migration cuts remain heavily debated among economists, migration experts, business groups and policymakers.

Critics argue lower migration can reduce labour supply, tax and visa revenue, population growth, consumer spending and business activity, particularly in industries that rely heavily on migrant workers.

A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education.

The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Debate over migration's impact on housing has also intensified in recent years. While higher migration can increase demand for homes, some experts argue migrant workers are also needed to address labour shortages in the construction sector.

In September, Burke said migration cuts would inevitably come with economic trade-offs and warned no industry would be immune from their effects.

"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he told SBS News.

"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure — as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."

Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.

One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which they say will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

title: 'Open the gates': Hellas boss calls for A-League admission after stunning final win
text:
in brief The South Melbourne Hellas have won the Australia Cup for the first time.

The 1-1 final came down to a penalty shootout in front of a sold-out crowd on Saturday night.

South Melbourne FC's co-president has said the nation's A-League might be knocking on his team's door after it became the first National Premier Leagues (NPL) side to win the Australia Cup, beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotionally charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic football history, former National Soccer League (NSL) powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time, then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at the Melbourne Rectangular Stadium.

It was the biggest moment in 22 years for South, commonly known as the Hellas, a reference to Hellenic (the native Greek name for Greece) to honour the large post-war Greek-Australian community that founded and supported the club.

The team was locked out of top-flight football alongside other NSL clubs when that league folded in 2024, and has long craved an A-League licence.

Bill Papastergiadis, South Melbourne FC's co-president, is confident his squad's performance on Saturday night will strengthen their chances of being granted entry to the nation's top tier of football.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We will be knocking on the A-League's door, or is the A-League knocking on South's door? Not sure what it is at the moment."

"Football needs to open the gates to allow clubs like South in and bring the passion back."

Those sentiments were echoed by the club's coach, Sinisa Cohadzic.

"I really cannot find any excuse not to see this club to play in the A-League," Cohadzic said.

"You talk about the A-League, the resources that they have and we have — it’s probably on par, and that’s why our players are able to compete."

South Melbourne captain Marco Janković said: "If you were someone that is in Europe [with] no idea what clubs they were, you wouldn’t know who's the A-League team — I think that’s something we noticed and it's very special".

'Surpasses even the most beautiful dreams'

South's stunning win came after Cohadzic urged his players to seize their chance in their 54th game this season, after losing the OFC Pro League final to Auckland FC.

"I said to them that tonight sometimes the reality surpasses even the most beautiful dreams, and tonight was one of those nights," he said.

"It was one of those nights where they had to believe that they can get a result."

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South Melbourne goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line — but then saved the re-take too.

"I remember in January when the club said we want to win the Australia Cup. I said 'you guys, that would be crazy'," Lopez said.

"Now we are the champions."

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South Melbourne great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, South have succeeded where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of the stadium, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskás and John Margaritis.

"You guys have stuck with us for 20 years, playing in the NPL and you've shown tonight what this future holds for this great club," Janković said.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Santos' poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

Hellas fans erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

"We were not surprised by the stadium, by the environment ... it was a proper Australia Cup the way it should be," Savarese said.

"I think it will be remembered as one of the most iconic.

"Unfortunately, on our side, I wish we lifted the trophy."

title: Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Passwords are supposed to keep us safe. Instead, they can leave us jumping through hoops just to end up less protected than where we started.

For years, we've been told a "strong" password needs a capital letter, a number, and a special character. But the rules designed to make passwords harder to crack were based on logic instead of evidence. It also made them harder to remember—pushing people to reuse the same passwords or make predictable changes.

That password paradox forced a rethink of one of the internet's most familiar security rituals almost ten years ago, and even one of the people who helped popularise the rules acknowledged they didn't work.

When William "Bill" Burr was a mid-level manager at the United States' National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), he was tasked with writing guidance on electronic authentication and password security.

That advice, published in 2004, helped cement the now-familiar idea that passwords should meet complexity requirements, including minimum length and a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters.

In 2017, Burr told The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) he regretted much of the guidance.

In the end, it was probably too complicated for a lot of folks to understand very well, and the truth is, it was barking up the wrong tree.

"It just drives people bananas," he said at the time.

When NIST updated its password guidance that same year, it moved away from some of those requirements, advising organisations against mandatory character-composition rules and routine password expiration.

Nearly a decade later, however, those rules remain common across websites and workplaces. So what does the evidence tell us about what actually makes a password secure?

The first computer passwords

The term password dates back to the late 1700s, and the idea of a secret phrase or access code to control entry goes back even further.

The first widely recognised computer password emerged in the early 1960s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as researchers worked on a system that let multiple people share access to a single computer.

In 1961, computer scientist Fernando Corbató led a project that developed the Compatible Time-Sharing System, or CTSS.

Fernando Corbató pioneered the use of computer passwords in the early 1960s. Source: Supplied / MIT Museum

Like a telephone exchange, the system let multiple users access a computer at the same time. But because they were sharing one machine, researchers needed a way to separate users and protect their individual files.

The password offered a simple solution: each user could have a secret string of characters controlling access to their files.

Corbató would later describe passwords as "kind of a nightmare" in a 2014 WSJ interview.

Why password complexity rules can backfire

Lorrie Cranor, a computer scientist and cybersecurity researcher at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania, tells SBS News passwords are "not a terrible idea" in a world where you have just one or two passwords.

But now we have the problem that we all have many passwords, because we have many accounts.

The premise behind password-composition rules was straightforward: if people were required to use a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, their passwords would be harder for attackers to guess.

But when those rules were first developed, evidence on how people would respond was limited.

NIST's initial guidelines also included a caveat: "Unfortunately, we do not have much data on the passwords users choose under particular rules."

It wasn't due to a lack of effort. In his 2017 interview, Burr said he even asked NIST's computer administrators to view actual passwords on their network, but they reportedly refused because of privacy concerns. The authors were therefore left to rely heavily on logic about how users might behave.

Researcher Lorrie Cranor's 'Security Blanket' features 1,000 of the most common passwords exposed in the 2009 RockYou breach. Source: Supplied / Lorrie Cranor

Since then, research has shown that the human response to password complexity is more complex.

A 2021 study from James Cook University found that increasing the number of password complexity rules did not necessarily produce stronger passwords and could increase user frustration.

It also found that users adopted strategies to make passwords easier to remember, including reusing passwords.

Why password reuse is a security problem

There are many ways to make a password weak, but reusing it across multiple services is one of the biggest risks.

Troy Hunt has seen many bad passwords. In 2013, he created Have I Been Pwned, a service that allows people to check whether their email address has appeared in a known data breach.

"As the internet came along, we already had these well-established principles that a password is memorable; it's something that you can type in," he tells SBS News.

"That came from an era where you needed things like physical presence in order to access services."

Troy Hunt (left) created Have I Been Pwned in 2013 to help people check whether their email address has been exposed in a data breach. Source: AP / Carolyn Kaster

But the internet changed the scale of the problem. People now have passwords for email, banking, shopping, social media, work systems and countless other services.

Hunt says the path of least resistance for people trying to make memorable passwords is to make them reusable.

NIST's 2017 guidance recommended checking passwords against lists of previously compromised passwords, as well as common and predictable choices, rather than relying solely on composition rules.

Shortly after, Hunt expanded his site to include a password checker.

Reused passwords are risky because once a password is exposed in a data breach, it's not only that breached service that is at risk.

Chances are it's going to be the same password that they use to buy that T-shirt or something online as they use to log onto the corporate network.

"And maybe the only thing that'll be different is the number on the end, depending on how many times they've had to rotate it," Hunt says.

NIST's current guidance recommends that organisations block commonly used, expected or compromised passwords rather than relying solely on rules about the types of characters a password contains.

What makes a good password policy?

When Carnegie Mellon University updated its password policy to include more complexity requirements, Cranor was already studying privacy and security usability.

So when her colleagues came to her complaining about the difficulty of the new requirements, she saw an opportunity.

Cranor and her team started studying password policies, hoping to answer a simple question: what is the best password policy an organisation can have?

"We wrote 20 papers and finally came up with the answer," she says.

The answer wasn't to include more special characters or numbers. Instead, the research pointed towards giving users more freedom by using an add-on to assess password strength.

The team developed an evidence-based password strength meter that assesses a password as it is created, rather than simply checking whether it meets a predetermined mix of characters.

It can also check the potential password against a list of common or exposed passwords to limit reuse.

You can put this on the web browser so that people are creating the password on the browser and are not sending the password over the internet.

"Of course, I know no organisations that are actually doing this."

Why companies still use password complexity rules

Jose-Miguel Bello Villarino is a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney Law School. He says technical standards can have misleading names.

"Technical standards are agreements in the industry among the dominant players in the way technical goods or processes are developed in the future," he tells SBS News.

"The tricky bit is that if it's something that is not legally mandated as a technical standard that has to be implemented, the people developing the things need to see a value in changing the way they're doing things."

The exception is when the change in standards relates to a safety risk.

"When it's a safety-related issue, and the standard has been adapted to these kinds of new circumstances, and you do not use that new standard, what you're risking is liability, because you are not meeting the standard," he says.

Even then, if one standards body adopts new guidelines, several different standards bodies must also update theirs for organisations to be able to make changes while remaining compliant with the relevant industry body.

Researcher Lorrie Cranor turned her bad-password fabric design into a range of dresses, including long-sleeved and formal versions, to raise awareness about password security. Source: Supplied / Lorrie Cranor

Cranor says security is about balancing risk with cost and benefit.

"There are a lot of security standards that companies follow and they're not all tied actually to the NIST guidelines," she says.

There's no perfect system, but if you're a security manager and you are appearing to be relaxing your requirements and then there's a breach, you're going to get the blame.

"Even if that's not true."

Hunt agrees. He says retaining the older rules often comes down to a "compliance officer with a checklist".

"A lot of security guidance has evolved, particularly in the last nine years since NIST put out their guidance. But a lot of computer systems and a lot of compliance regimes have taken a very long time to catch up as well."

So, what makes a strong password?

Cranor's main advice for making good passwords is not to make them yourself. Instead, she says to use a password manager to generate and store them.

You are not good at generating random passwords; your password manager is.

Hunt says the best passwords are the "ones you can't remember".

There is a small subset of passwords where this advice doesn't help, such as the password for your laptop or the one used to access your password manager.

Hunt describes this as distinguishing "what do you actually need to remember versus what do you need to be able to retrieve".

For the passwords you actually need to remember, contemporary advice generally favours length over arbitrary complexity.

One way to get that length is to use passphrases, but the key is to make the phrase hard to guess and ideally, random.

"Except the problem with random is that most of us are not very good at remembering things that actually are random," Cranor says.

"If you are, then do that. Roll a dice, pull from a hat, make something actually random."

To avoid this kind of predictability, Cranor recommends taking a memorable sentence that makes sense to you and using the first two letters of each word to create a new string, with some punctuation or a digit added somewhere in the middle.

And where its possible, Hunt suggests choosing non-password alternatives like passkeys. But their uptake has been slow, and he warns people will still have to deal with passwords for many years to come.

They will still be there because they will take a very, very long time to die.

title: Flydubai co-pilot drifted towards 'extremism and terrorism' while studying at RMIT
text:
In brief Omani national Hammam al-Hammami become acquainted with individuals from a group called "My Centre", run by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza".

The co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month.

The Omani flydubai co-pilot who was accused of trying to crash a plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport last month was radicalised at an Australian mosque while studying in Melbourne in 2017, according to the United Arab Emirates attorney general.

Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, 29, allegedly tried to hijack flight FZ1073 with 182 people onboard travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September before passengers and crew intervened.

A statement by UAE attorney general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi shared on UAE government social media said al-Hammami's radicalisation happened when was a student at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During mosque visits, al-Hammami became acquainted with individuals associated with a centre known as "My Centre".

The statement said al-Hammami had revealed the centre was managed by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza" and allegedly received support from an association linked to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Al-Hammami, who joined flydubai in January, had previously worked for several airlines in different countries, the UAE's investigation had found.

"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," al-Shamsi added.

The investigation found there were signs of al-Hammami drifting towards "extremism and terrorism" as early as ‌2017, while he was studying in Australia.

Royal Air Maroc has said that he underwent three months of training there in 2025 but that his application to work for the airline afterwards was rejected.

title: Positive or problematic? Here's how much fibre you really need
text:
IN BRIEF: Fibre-maxxing has swept the algorithm, but it has multiple health benefits.

Experts say it's important fibre is consumed as food, and not supplements.

Are you getting enough fibre in your diet?

The recommended daily fibre intake is 30g for men and 25g for women, but Australian men and women consume on average about 21g and 18g of fibre per day, respectively. So, you're probably not.

Dietitians have been calling for Australians to increase their fibre intake for decades, and now the challenge has made its way to social media.

Enter the fibre-maxxer: A person committed to hitting, and even exceeding, their daily fibre target.

Online fibre-maxxers promote eating more fruits and vegetables and increasing dietary fibre intake by adding seeds, grains and vegetables to regular foods. This includes putting chia seeds in soft drinks, beans on avocado toast, grains in homemade bread, or adding a cup of legumes to rice.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Can you have too much fibre?

Program director of human nutrition and associate professor at Adelaide University, Evangeline Mantzioris, said that while fibre-maxxing was probably "one of the more positive" social media-fuelled food trends, some elements could be "problematic".

"We actually do need to increase the amount of fibre in our diet," Mantzioris told SBS News.

She said the daily intake suggestion of 25 to 30g per day was based on attaining the best health outcomes, including a reduction of colon cancer, "which is one of the most preventable diseases we have".

"But I understand some are suggesting intakes up to 50 grams a day, possibly more, and there isn't a lot of good evidence that having such extremely high levels may provide any additional benefits."

While there is no upper limit on how much fibre you can eat, more fibre means your body produces more flatulence.

"One of the biggest problems, I guess, is gas, right? No one wants to be gassy out in public."

Another issue, Mantzioris said, is fluid intake.

It was imperative to drink a healthy amount of fluids throughout the day, as without fluids, high fibre can cause constipation, rather than ease it.

"I describe it as it's a bit like trying to clean the bathroom with a dry sponge or a wet sponge. The wet sponge is going to work a lot better than the dry sponge," she said.

"Any increase in fibre will result in an increase in wind, and what we normally tell people to do is to do it slowly."

Foods like hemp seeds, quinoa, nuts, and legumes are high in dietary fibre. Source: Getty / Tanja Ivanova

Don't "go from nothing to 40 grams of fibre in one day". Instead, Mantzioris said, gradually increase high-fibre foods in your diet. This will also help ensure it is a "sustainable" transition for your gut microbiome, the complex community of trillions of microorganisms that live in your digestive tract.

"We know that the bacteria in our gut use that fibre for their survival, and we know that the fibre that comes from whole foods like fruit, vegetables, legumes, beans, nuts, and seeds gives you the healthiest type of microbiome possible", as opposed to the bacteria that thrive on "sometimes foods", which are unhealthy for your body.

"So it's sort of like this lovely symbiotic relationship between your bacteria and you, and the more healthy food you give them, the better off they are, and the better off you are."

Why fibre should come from food

"It's all about balance," Mantzioris said, stressing that fibre intake should come from food, not supplements, which she said some fibremaxxing influencers might be recommending.

"By using supplements, you're missing out on all of the additional nutrients that are in the foods that they originally come from."

She said the best way to avoid "overdosing" on fibre would be to get it from food.

"And get it from a range of different foods — there are a lot of different types of fibres, and they each play a different role in our bodies."

"It's important to eat beans, to eat fruit, eat vegetables, and to eat cereals, to get the maximum benefits from all the different types of fibres, as well as the nutrients that come with all those foods that we know promote health," she said.

What is fibre?

Fibre is a nutrient found in many foods that reduces your risk of chronic disease and keeps your digestive system healthy.

Adequate dietary fibre is essential for proper gut function. It has also been related to risk reduction for some chronic diseases, including heart disease, certain cancers and diabetes.

There are three kinds of fibre: soluble fibre, which slows down digestion, like oats and barley; insoluble fibre, like whole grains, which bulks your stool and speeds up the movement of food through your digestive tract; and resistant starch, found in boiled and cooled potatoes, which ferments in your gut and acts as a prebiotic to feed beneficial bacteria.

Mantzioris said there were "a few reasons" why fibre intake was so consistently low in Australia.

Only about 5 per cent of Australians are meeting the minimum requirements for vegetables in their diet, at 5 serves a day.

Chia seeds, native to Central America, are popular amongst online fibremaxxers due to their exceptionally high fibre content Source: Getty / Stefania Pelfini la Waziya

"And of course, fibre vegetables are a great source of fibre," Mantzioris said.

She pointed to the ever-increasing popularity of high-protein diets, or "the protein craze".

"When you're consuming more of one food, you're dropping out another essential food group, which is providing you with essential nutrients."

"They're focusing on their protein intake, and we know that roughly 98 per cent of Australians meet their protein requirement".

Beans, she said, were a great example of a high-protein food with multiple benefits.

"The benefit of that protein source is that it also gives you the fibre, and all the antioxidants that we need to fight disease, to reduce oxidative stress in the body and reduce inflammation."

"Every different colour you have in the plant foods represents a different nutrient that's useful for the body."

Finally, she said, "There's an aversion to carbohydrates in our society."

"People see carbohydrates as the problem food when it comes to trying to manage their weight — and all of the carbohydrate-rich foods also provide us with a lot of fibre."

title: Two goals but no win for Matildas in Germany friendly
text:
in brief Australia lost 4-2 in an away game against Germany.

The match was an international friendly ahead of next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

The Matildas may count the cost of an error-riddled 4-2 defeat to an understrength Germany after star striker Sam Kerr emerged from the game complaining of ankle soreness.

With limited international windows remaining before next year's FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil, Friday's (Saturday AEDT) clash against the world No.3 in Karlsruhe was crucial.

Headlines before the game were dominated by the absence of Manchester City star Mary Fowler (personal reasons), and she was missed as the Germans scored the opening two goals.

But captain Kerr's header on the stroke of halftime helped the visitors close the deficit before the home team's Camilla Kuver scored in the 83rd minute.

Striker Holly McNamara did find a late consolation goal for the Matildas, but Chelsea midfielder Sjoeke Nusken dashed any hopes of a draw.

Most concerningly, Kerr was taken off in the 64th minute after her ankle was trodden on minutes before her goal.

The skipper played down the severity of the injury, but added that she wasn't comfortable.

"I came in with a bit of a sore ankle," Kerr told Paramount +.

"I always plan to come off around the 60th, 70th minute. So nothing about the ankle (contributed to) coming off, but it's pretty sore now."

For Germany, the victory came despite the two-time world champions missing a plethora of stars, including captain Giulia Gwinn (ankle) and Liverpool forward Vivien Endemann (calf).

Australia will rue the missed opportunity to capitalise on their opponents' absences as a win would have helped them remain firmly in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

"The biggest thing for us is we have to make sure that any time we retrieve the ball or we have situations where we have the opportunity to win the ball, we have to keep it better," coach Joe Montemurro said.

"We probably created a lot of chances for Germany, with a lot of our technical errors which we know now that we can't get away with at this top level."

Despite the result, the Matildas will have something to celebrate as defender Tori Tumeth made her debut off the bench in the second half.

World No.15 Australia sent an early warning shot when Ellie Carpenter put in a dangerous cross to Kerr, but Germany upped the ante afterwards.

Defender Carlotta Wamser lofted a cross to Franziska Kett, and she used her head to guide the ball onto the feet of forward Melissa Kossler.

Seven minutes later Kossler stormed down the field and thumped the ball into the bottom left corner.

But in the dying moments of the first half, Carpenter fired a cross onto the head of Kerr and the striker closed the deficit to 2-1 at the break.

Midfielder Clare Wheeler had an opportunity go begging in the 56th minute when her shot rattled onto the crossbar.

Bayern Munich's Linda Dallmann dispatched a corner for a header by defender Kuver, and she nodded the ball past Mackenzie Arnold.

In injury time, Caitlin Foord poked the ball to McNamara, and she scored. However, Nusken whacked the ball into the bottom right corner to seal the victory.

"We can be satisfied," Kossler said.

"We set ourselves some tactical goals, wanted to try something out, and were able to implement them successfully for the most part."

The latest results add another layer of intrigue to Horizon’s broader Gum Creek development ambitions, which are built around a substantial gold inventory and an established mining district with a long production history. Gum Creek, 640km northeast of Perth, is a classic brownfields revival story. More than one million ounces have been produced from 37 open pits and three underground mines, while a 110-person camp, operational airstrip and extensive haul roads give Horizon a substantial development head start. Operations ceased in 2005, when gold was languishing at A$560 an ounce. Today’s much stronger gold market gives Horizon a very different launchpad. The company’s July definitive feasibility study (DFS) outlined a robust plan for a new 2.4-million-tonne-a-year processing plant at Gidgee, underpinned by a 728,000-ounce ore reserve. It envisages a 10-year operation producing an average of 88,000 ounces a year, peaking at 114,000 ounces in year two and recovering 880,000 ounces over the mine life. It forecasts pre-production capital of A$350M and an all-in sustaining cost of A$2,995 an ounce. The real kicker is that this starter case draws on only a fraction of Gum Creek’s global resource of 37.97 million tonnes grading 1.89g/t for 2.3 million ounces of gold. A 416,000-ounce free-milling underground resource and the 400,000-ounce Wilsons sulphide deposit also sit outside the current mine plan, offering further growth beyond the DFS case.

Snook, Cobia and Alma May are similarly excluded from the initial mine plan, so success across the three prospects could add significant scale to the project’s already substantial gold inventory. Alongside its work, Horizon is targeting a final investment decision on the company’s main Gum Creek development in the second quarter of 2027, with first gold targeted in the second half of 2028. Horizon has a solid DFS in its back pocket and high-grade hits emerging beyond the initial mine plan at Cobia, Alma May and Snook. Josh Frydenberg has criticised the direction of the Liberal Party, arguing it must change in the face of an existential threat. The former treasurer, who was considered a future Liberal leader before losing his seat in 2022, has stoked speculation he will run again with the release of a new memoir, which includes criticism the party has lost touch with its roots, as well as his proposals for policy remedies. Former treasurer Josh Frydenberg has left the door open to a political comeback. Eddie Jim The intervention creates a fresh headache for Taylor, who immediately shut down Frydenberg’s suggestion that a Coalition government should raise the GST to offset income and business tax cuts. Taylor returned to parliament this week after addressing the annual Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane on Saturday, where he was heckled by One Nation loyalists in the audience and ridiculed by the next speaker, Pauline Hanson.

Advertisement

On Sunday night, Frydenberg said Taylor was copping criticism from “lots of corners” by people saying the party needed to do better. “The polls are showing that the Liberal Party is at an all-time low,” Frydenberg told 60 Minutes. “And so, things have to change. Because there’s something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces.” Treasurer Jim Chalmers exploited Frydenberg’s criticism of the party’s direction during question time to mock Taylor. Chalmers took a Dorothy Dixer about Labor’s economic management when he turned to the debt left after Frydenberg’s time in government, and the former member for Kooyong’s latest pitch to lift the GST. “The leader of the opposition (Angus Taylor) is being stalked from the inside by the member for Canning (Andrew Hastie). He’s being stalked from the outside by the failed former member for Kooyong (Frydenberg),” Chalmers said.

Advertisement

Chalmers said shadow treasurer Tim Wilson had also floated increasing the GST to 20 per cent in his first speech to parliament. Taylor quickly nixed the suggestion on Sunday when asked about Frydenberg’s proposal. Frydenberg has denied his book was a pitch for the prime ministership, but when asked if he still had aspirations to lead the country, said he had not closed that door. “I don’t need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away,” he said. A political comeback for the former treasurer would involve a protracted campaign for a seat with weak preference flows that the Liberals failed to recapture in 2025. He would also have to win a preselection contest, which some senior Victorian Liberal operatives unsupportive of Frydenberg want resolved by the first quarter of next year. But Frydenberg’s supporters suggest he will seek to delay an announcement on his candidacy until the latest possible moment, as he assesses the political terrain and the likelihood of winning the seat.

Advertisement

The Coalition is trailing Labor and One Nation in the polls, and Taylor is behind Anthony Albanese and Pauline Hanson as preferred prime minister, though he edged up 1 point in the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson, who in 2025 became the first Liberal to reclaim a seat from a teal independent, said on Monday he had no issue with Frydenberg putting himself forward at the next election. “I think it’s always good to have candidates who want to step up and run and make sure we pick up seats so that Angus Taylor can be prime minister of this country,” Wilson told Radio National. Fellow Coalition frontbenchers Andrew Bragg and Angie Bell, who Frydenberg reveals in his book were part of a meeting of moderates in 2021 to discuss concerns about then prime minister Scott Morrison’s leadership, have urged the former treasurer to run.

Advertisement

In the 60 Minutes interview, Frydenberg said he stood by his decision not to challenge Morrison for the leadership at that time. “During my time in office, there were numerous changes of prime ministership and leadership of the Liberal Party, and in each time, I stood by the incumbent, and I don’t regret that,” he said. Frydenberg said he was more disappointed by the multiple ministries scandal, in which Morrison secretly swore himself into the portfolios of several colleagues, including Frydenberg’s. Related Article Political leadership Monique Ryan says Frydenberg focused on the past, amid accusations of a ‘toxic’ campaign “I was angry about it, and I felt undermined. It was completely unnecessary for him to do that, and I think a lot of colleagues felt blindsided,” he said.

“I made it very clear that it was unnecessary, and he said to me that he would have made the same decision again, and I said you can’t be serious. So that’s something that he’ll obviously have to explain for himself. But it has damaged our relationship.” Current Kooyong MP, independent Monique Ryan, on Monday said she was not bothered who the Liberal Party put up as a candidate at the next election. She added that Frydenberg had his chance with voters. Independent MP Monique Ryan said Kooyong had already rejected Frydenberg. Luis Enrique Ascui “He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change,” Ryan told Seven’s Sunrise. “People were unhappy with his economic management. People were very unhappy with the way that he punched down on Victoria during the COVID years. I’m not sure what has changed since that time that Mr Frydenberg now thinks that the community will welcome him back with open arms.”

She accused Frydenberg of being too focused on ongoing prime ministerial ambitions instead of his community. “He doesn’t speak much about Kooyong, and that’s the part of the world that I’m most focused on.” After initially avoiding Frydenberg’s claims last week that her supporters had run a campaign rife with personal abuse, Ryan said on Monday she rejected that characterisation. “It does not match with my own recollections or the recollections of the more than 2000 people who volunteered with me. As Victorians start to lock in to the choice before them at next month’s state election, the political contest is being fought overwhelmingly on the Coalition’s preferred ground, with the economy, financial management and crime the dominant issues on voters’ minds. The latest Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead shows that Premier Ben Carroll’s personal popularity has taken a 9-point dive to minus 11, suggesting voters have weighed up Labor’s newest leader and aren’t convinced by what they see. Premier Ben Carroll is being dogged by a new problem – sinking personal popularity. Jason South Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, by contrast, has established herself as one of Australia’s most popular political leaders, with her already strong personal likeability climbing 4 percentage points to 23. Voting intentions are little changed since last month’s Resolve poll, with Labor stuck on primary support of 25 per cent, the Coalition unmoved on 28 and One Nation steady on 23 per cent.

Advertisement

While these numbers, if replicated on November 28, would almost certainly deliver a change of government, it is less clear whether the Coalition would be able to form a majority government without the help of One Nation or another minor party. The only significant movers in this latest poll are the Victorian Greens, who for the first time in three years are showing signs of electoral growth with a 3-point boost to their primary support. This has come at the expense of independents, who attracted support from only 4 per cent of the 1000 respondents surveyed. If replicated on election day, this could deliver stronger preference flows to Labor in some seats. Early polling in Victoria opens in just over six weeks.

Advertisement

Resolve founder Jim Reed said one of the key findings of the survey was that people were now paying closer attention. “Fewer and fewer voters are telling us they are uncommitted each month, and the number of people undecided on their preferred leader is also dropping, which is evidence that they are starting to pay attention and lock in,” he said. “Victorians were willing to give Carroll a fair go, but after a few months they are increasingly unconvinced. His net likeability and preferred premier metrics are both down. And Wilson is benefiting from that.” The most encouraging news for the Coalition from this survey, other than the level of personal support for Wilson, is that its areas of perceived relative strength – economic and financial management, and crime and policing – are at the top of voters’ priority lists.

Advertisement

When asked what their highest priority issue was for deciding how to vote, 33 per cent of respondents nominated the state’s economy and finances, while 24 per cent said crime and policing. The second-highest priority – the traditional Labor strength of hospitals and health services – was nominated by 12 per cent of respondents. When asked to nominate things that will most influence their vote from a list of more specific issues and policy announcements, 27 per cent chose government spending and debt, while 21 per cent went for youth crime. Greens voters nominated artificial intelligence and data centres as their biggest vote-shaping concern. The survey was conducted between October 6 and October 10, in the aftermath of One Nation’s Victorian policy and campaign launch, which featured a grab bag of uncosted promises.

Advertisement

The boldest policy announcement of the week was Jess Wilson’s $1.27 billion promise to halve the elective surgery waiting list by booking 25,000 additional patients into private hospitals to have surgery on the public tab. This masthead on Monday revealed the policy involved bringing forward $1.1 billion of borrowed money earmarked for future capital investment over the next decade to cover the cost of the urgent surgeries. Previously unpublished budget figures show the opposition’s accounting would create an $880 million shortfall in its election costings. Carroll leapt on the revelation on Monday, telling 3AW, “The opposition leader says she knows everything and can do both treasury and leader. That has now seen a billion-dollar budget black hole in her costings on health.” Wilson defended the credibility of her costings by saying she would not be “lectured by the Labor Party on economic mismanagement in this state”.

Advertisement

“Budgets don’t just look at one policy in isolation. They don’t just look at the spend of one policy in isolation. They look at policies – that’s both savings and expenditure – in aggregate over those four years, taking into account the net debt position, looking at the forecast, and of course, the operating position in the state,” Wilson said. She repeated her goal of returning the state’s finances to cash surplus by 2032 if elected in November, and said it was only at this point – when the state is raising more in revenue than it spends on operating expenses and capital investments – that reducing net debt becomes possible. Jess Wilson, pictured with Nationals leader Danny O’Brien, has defended the costings behind her policy for public patients to access elective surgery through private hospitals. Luis Enrique Ascui Reed said the electoral challenge before the Coalition – to gain an additional 16 seats required to form majority government – remained a big ask, but noted the dominant issues and the respective likeability of the leaders are pointing in the right direction for the Liberal and National parties. “Things like potholes and the Suburban Rail Loop are handy icons for voters to talk about, but our polling is telling us that the foundational issues of economic health, debt and crime are what’s driving votes,” Reed said. “This is Coalition ground.”

title: The Wallabies have faced the music. Can they now change their Bledisloe tune?
text:

Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The Wallabies have faced the music. Can they now change their Bledisloe tune? Monday press conferences after a Bledisloe Cup defeat would have to rank among the least appealing assignments for any Wallabies player. Particularly when Saturday’s 50-19 capitulation against the All Blacks at Eden Park marked Australia’s 12th consecutive defeat to their trans-Tasman rivals. Loading On the second floor of a hotel across the road from Accor Stadium at Sydney Olympic Park, the venue for Saturday’s dead-rubber Bledisloe clash, Wallabies fullback Tom Wright was the one chosen to explain how Australia had conceded so many points. “The guys were obviously really disappointed with the result,” Wright said. “The group came together on Sunday morning [to] face the music.”

Advertisement

Face the music? From coaches? Or senior players laying down the law? “The music of the scoreboard,” Wright said. “No one wants to be on the receiving end of 50 points. No one wants to be on the receiving end of a loss. At 17-14 [in front], we’re right in the contest, and the game was there to be taken. We knew the opportunity was there for us. Tom Wright of Australia reacts to the loss. Getty Images “We felt like all the guns were loaded, and we had the ammunition to fire shots and win the game. We didn’t. That’s the music that we’re talking about. You can be internally so driven to win and when you don’t … that’s the disappointment you’ve got to face.” For all the optimism generated by a six-game unbeaten streak before last weekend, including a surprise win over the Springboks, the broader Australian sporting public ultimately judges the Wallabies on one thing: whether they can beat the All Blacks.

Advertisement

And when it comes to New Zealand, the same old problems keep resurfacing. Some would have turned on the television expecting a spirited second-half performance, but all they got was a botched Australian lineout deep in Kiwi territory that became the catalyst for an All Blacks onslaught that turned a contest into another humiliating defeat. It was a familiar script, even if the Wallabies had spent much of the first half threatening to rewrite it. The aerial contest wasn’t a contest. Inevitably, out came the same questions that get rolled out every year. What is it about the All Blacks? Is there a mental inferiority complex when it comes to Eden Park?

Advertisement

Wright, one of Australia’s best on Saturday after scoring the opening try on Saturday, is not one for magic solutions. “If I had the golden egg answer, it’d be pretty handy,” Wright said. “But I certainly don’t think there are any mental scars. Wallabies head coach Les Kiss. Getty Images “They’re not a poor team. The narrative will always be that ... we haven’t got our hands on the Bledisloe Cup, and we haven’t got a win against them [in 12 attempts]. “We know that the Bledisloe Cup remains across the ditch. We can’t carry that disappointment into the rest of this week because it’s not going to help us win on Saturday, is it?”

Advertisement

Former Wallaby Tim Horan spoke for plenty of frustrated Australian supporters on Sunday when asked on Channel Nine about the familiar narrative that the Wallabies would “learn” from their mistakes across the ditch. “I just don’t like hearing, ‘oh we’re going to learn from this’. I think Aussies are sick of getting beaten by the All Blacks,” Horan said. Loading Add Wright to that list. But for the doom and gloom around Australia’s inability to reclaim the Bledisloe Cup, a drought now stretching 24 years, the Wallabies have promised themselves they won’t spend the week feeling sorry for themselves.

Advertisement

The trophy is gone for another year, but Saturday presents an opportunity to restore some pride and avoid a clean sweep. Related Article Australian rugby Box clever: Wallabies say accuracy and urgency keys to combatting All Blacks’ aerial dominance Australia and New Zealand also face each other in the pool stages at next year’s Rugby World Cup at the same venue. There will be an element of wanting to land an early psychological blow ahead of a game that really matters. “You can be disappointed, but you’ve got to pick up the pieces pretty quickly to be able to move on and give ourselves a good opportunity this Saturday,” Wright said. “The guys are pretty keen to get back on the horse.”

Advertisement

One player unavailable for the Wallabies’ final match before their European spring tour is Jordan Petaia, who missed the Auckland clash after suffering a syndesmosis injury at training last week. Petaia is expected to be sidelined for about a month after being caught in an awkward tackle involving several Wallabies players, including Max Jorgensen, in the lead-up to the first Bledisloe Test.

title: They’ve been a lost cause for 10 years. The Wanderers may have finally worked out why
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerA-League Men They’ve been a lost cause for 10 years. The Wanderers may have finally worked out why Vince Rugari October 12, 2026 — 3:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. As an actor, Ufuk Talay makes a very good football coach. The new Western Sydney Wanderers boss is the frontman of a cheeky commercial for the A-League club’s sponsor, property management group Starr Partners, in which he pokes fun at his controversial defection from arch-rivals Sydney FC, setting the tone for a spicy season-opening derby on Friday night. View post on X It’s filled with unsubtle Easter eggs - Talay replacing sky blue things with red and black, nods to famous footballing turncoats such as Luis Figo and Sol Campbell - and ends with Milos Ninkovic, the most high-profile player to have switched from Sydney to the Wanderers, welcoming him to the neighbourhood. It’s also the hardest thing Talay reckons he’s ever done.

Advertisement

“I’m not an actor, I’ll tell you that much,” he laughed. “It was actually quite enjoyable, but very stressful at the same time. I did so many takes … they’d go, ‘That was excellent, but can you just smile at the end, please?’ I’m just trying to remember the line, not remember about smiling. New Wanderers football director Mal Impiombato and coach Ufuk Talay at the club’s Rooty Hill base. James Brickwood “Overall, I think it was good fun. I think it adds a bit of banter to the derby that we play in the first round.” It remains to be seen how Talay is received by Sydney fans at Allianz Stadium, which is tracking for a crowd of over 35,000. Many of them were happy to see the back of Talay anyway, and have since embraced the club’s new direction under Patrick Kisnorbo.

Advertisement

The Wanderers faithful, meanwhile, are daring to dream again after a productive off-season, in which they went unbeaten in trial matches against A-League opposition (they were knocked out of the Australia Cup on penalties by Melbourne Victory) and suffered their only defeat to visiting Chelsea, of all teams. Their squad looks decent enough, but then again, that’s never really been the problem. The only defeat the Wanderers have tasted in regulation time this pre-season was against Chelsea. Getty With all due respect to Talay, the club’s ninth coach since the departure of inaugural boss Tony Popovic, in which time they’ve played finals only twice, he is not the most important appointment the Wanderers have made. Finally, they have addressed a key off-field vacuum above the coach and filled it with one of the game’s most respected operators.

Advertisement

Step forward, Mal Impiombato, the club’s inaugural director of football. His name may not resonate widely, but his track record suggests he could be exactly what the Wanderers need. Ufuk Talay during his days at Sydney FC. Getty Images Out of a job after the collapse of Western United, having essentially served as the architect of the defunct club’s productive football department, Impiombato has spent the last few months trying to understand why one of Australian football’s biggest clubs has been punching below its weight for so long. His diagnosis was as straightforward as his proposed remedy, and it will not shock anyone: the Wanderers had the resources, facilities and talent, but their various football departments were operating in isolation, without a coherent strategy to connect them.

Advertisement

Since arriving in April, Impiombato has tried to bring their men’s, women’s, academy and even disability programs closer together, establishing clearer lines of communication and responsibility, as well as a common set of playing principles which will govern how any Wanderers team tries to approach any game, the profile of players who are brought into the club, and what kind of players they develop internally. “People think you’re going to add this whole new plethora of things that no one’s ever heard of before,” said Impiombato, who has also worked at two other A-League clubs as well as Football Australia. Ufuk Talay in the dugout for Sydney FC. Getty “There’s no groundbreaking thing that I wanted to bring in, outside of the fundamental basics of what makes teams successful, and that’s stability, structure and a bit of strategic direction and alignment to understand where we want to go and how we want to get there.” It’s boring, but hopefully, the outcomes won’t be.

Advertisement

If it wasn’t clear enough from the ad he fronted, Talay knows that the life of a coach is transient and insecure. The work done by Impiombato is intended to ensure that the Wanderers’ own identity is far less reliant on the identity of their coach, which is how Talay reckons it should be. “As much as I’m the coach of the team, I still believe that it should be a club-centred model, not a coach-centred model,” Talay said. “The coach comes in, and he goes, ‘No, no, we’ll scrap everything that you’ve done for the last year, the last five years, and we’ll restart and do it again.’ And I don’t think that actually works.” Even better for Talay, the presence of Impiombato provides him with something few of his predecessors have enjoyed: a layer of protection from chairman Paul Lederer and his board if results take a turn for the worse and their trigger fingers get itchy. “Having a football director that sits above me, between me and the board, gives me a buffer,” he said. “It’s very important to have a person like Mal, who’s a fantastic human being first and foremost. He’s the guy that will hopefully protect me when things aren’t going as well so that there’s no knee-jerk decisions, emotional decisions … it allows me to focus on my job.”

Advertisement

Of course, none of this guarantees success, and Wanderers fans have heard it all before. The past decade has been filled with false dawns, and Talay is the first to admit that their impressive pre-season results will be meaningless if they don’t show the same stuff when there are points on the line. Related Article Analysis

Australia Cup Let them in: South Melbourne just showed the A-League what it has been missing The real test begins on Friday night against the club Talay left behind, in front of a crowd that will be eager to see him fail. On his end, at least, there are no hard feelings. “Players make changes, coaches make changes. For me, home is where you’re at,” Talay said.

Advertisement

“This is what I do as a job to look after my family. The reality is I’m at Western Sydney at the moment, I’m very happy to be here, and I’ll do everything possible to help the group and help the club move forward, and hopefully bring some sort of success. “In a few years’ time, that might change again, and you’re somewhere else. That’s the nature of our game. You put your hat down and be ready to pick it up and move on to the next thing.” When that day comes, at least he’ll know which company to call.

The new visual results build on a spectacular maiden drilling campaign that recently delivered the headline hit of 18m at 7.31g/t gold from 63m in just the second hole drilled. Notably, that discovery hole also included a second, deeper zone of 16m grading 1.46g/t gold from 113m, along with an initial hole that landed a solid 23-metre intercept running 2.14g/t gold right from surface. Samples from the new hole are in transit and have been prioritised for a fast turnaround, with results expected before the end of this month. Assays for the previous holes drilled in the campaign are also at the laboratory, with results anticipated from early November.

′ Our focus is on building the geological evidence to assess the scale and continuity of the mineralisation.′ Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan The ongoing work forms part of Dalaroo’s maiden 24-hole, 4200-metre orientation program, the opening salvo in a much bigger 12,000-metre reverse circulation (RC) program targeting the Wilfred, Mag and Ali prospects at Bondoukou. So far, the company has completed 10 RC holes, totalling 2252m, across its Wilfred prospect. Dalaroo Metals chief executive officer John Morgan said: “Our first reported high-grade gold intersections at Wilfred established an exciting starting point for exploration at Gold Ridge. We are encouraged that hole has now encountered alteration, quartz-sulphide veining and a rock sequence comparable to that seen in the discovery hole. The immediate priority is to establish, through laboratory assays and follow-up drilling, whether these geological features are associated with further gold mineralisation and how the system is oriented.” The new hole was drilled north-west of the company’s original discovery holes along the interpreted 7km-long Gold Ridge corridor. Both holes intersected a similar package of rocks at broadly similar depths, despite being drilled more than a kilometre apart and in opposite directions. Dalaroo believes this apparent geological link-up could strongly indicate the scale of the mineralising system it has on its hands. The company is certainly not standing still, with the RC rig now setting up for a scissor hole, designed to intersect the new 34-metre alteration zone at depth and at a different angle to help define its orientation. After completing work at Wilfred, the rig will move on to test the nearby Ali and Mag prospects.

Advertisement

In parallel, a diamond drill rig is scheduled to mobilise to the project in mid-to-late October to begin follow-up work around the original high-grade discovery. The company is also finalising plans for an induced polarisation geophysics survey along the entire 7km-long Gold Ridge corridor to help prioritise additional drill targets. The Bondoukou project lies in the prolific Birimian greenstone belt, a rapidly emerging gold district just 35 kilometres from Endeavour Mining’s giant five-million-ounce Tanda-Iguela gold project. The belt also hosts a string of other multi-million-ounce gold deposits, making it one of Africa’s most well-endowed gold regions. While West Africa is the clear focus, Dalaroo is also advancing other projects in its portfolio. At its Blue Lagoon project in Greenland, the company is chasing rare earths, while closer to home, an induced-polarisation survey has firmed up several compelling drill targets at its Watheroo copper-nickel-PGE project in WA. After making a high-grade discovery with some of its earliest drill holes at Bondoukou, Dalaroo now has visual evidence that the system could extend for some distance. With a bevvy of assays due in the coming weeks and a suite of exploration activities kicking off, the market will likely be watching closely to see just how big this West African gold play could be. WA Premier Roger Cook says WA’s universities could sell land for housing to help fund a proposed three-way merger between Curtin, Murdoch and the University of Western Australia. Opposition to the merger has heated up after the WA government announced it would develop a business case to see whether a mega-university stacked up. More than two-thirds of university staff surveyed opposed the proposal Curtin University vice chancellor Harlene Hayne and the WA opposition have pointed to job losses and the blown out costs of the Adelaide University merger, which has reached more than $1 billion. The National Tertiary Education Union also released survey results in Monday that found 68.7 per cent of the 936 university staff surveyed opposed the proposal.

Advertisement

Cook sought to allay fears that taxpayers would be on the line for the merger costs by suggesting the universities could sell land. “We believe this should be not up to the WA taxpayer to foot all the bill,” he said. “They’ve got significant parcels of land, land which could be repurposed for housing, and so that’s an explicit objective of the steering committee.” He rejected opposition concerns the merger could cost the state between $1 billion to $2 billion. “By critics of the proposal, yes, it has [been estimated to coast $1 billion], but we have an explicit objective of the steering committee who are putting together the business case for this to be self-funding,” he said.

Advertisement

Related Article University Battle lines drawn as Curtin opposes WA’s mega-university plan The business case comes after two separate reports into the sector in 2023 and 2025 that called for a merger to create a more competitive university globally. Cook said the three-way merger was “preordained”. “We’ll look at the business case. If it stacks up, well, then obviously we’ll take the opportunities that come with it,” he said. “I believe this is an important reform. It’s important to make sure we have a world-class university from Western Australia, not only for our students, but for our economy.”

Advertisement

According to the union survey results, opposition to the merger was strongest at Curtin University at 75 per cent. Those opposed pointed to the disruption that followed the Adelaide University merger, the scale of likely job losses, and the size and complexity of the merged university. The tertiary union will be part of the steering committee and Curtin branch president Professor Scott Fitzgerald said he would be relaying the opposition. “That’s exactly the message I’ll be delivering as part of the steering committee. Beyond that, we’ll be using everything at our disposal to fight hard against a merger,” he said. “It’s highly concerning that the committee’s work is centred on a business case. Public universities exist to serve students, staff and the wider community. Any decision about their future should be through that focus, not a simplistic approach that puts profits over people.”

Advertisement

Murdoch University urged the state government to re-consider the merger in a statement released on Sunday. “The potential merger is at odds with the federal government’s approach to higher education policy as expressed through the Australian Universities Accord and the establishment of the Australian Tertiary Education Commission, which promotes a greater diversity of universities across Australia,” a spokeswoman said. “As we have stated continually throughout the merger debate, we believe Western Australia is best served by having four public universities, each with its own special characteristics.” The steering committee will be led by Fortescue deputy chair Mark Barnaba and medical researcher Professor Fiona Wood as deputy chair.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
